PUNCH is sometimes a great public in-
structor, and on many occasions the British
people have had reason to ba grateful to our
pleasant contemporary. Sometimes, however
the comical old gentleman is drawn out o
his natural pleasantness by his prejudices, and
occasionally he strikes about with his baton
in a wild sort of way, without seeming to
know exaotly what he would lie at. Of
course he must shoot folly and vice as they
fly, but when such a duty is undertaken in
the interest of the public it should be per-
formed with all requisite discrimination, and
with as little as possible of that spirit which
usually expresses itself in ugly names or
'vulgar insinuations. It is very easy to repre-
sent a man who takes any part in the discus-
sion of public questions as an "agitator," a de-
magogue, or by any other name which describes
him as a mercenary agent of mischief ; just
as any painter may be called a" dauber," or
any writer a " soribbler." But this is not the
language of gentlemen, nor is it ever used by
those who, in the ordinary controversies of
life, seek to triumph in a spirit of justice and
fair play.
These remarks have been called forth by
the cartoon which appeared a fortnight since
in Punch, relative to the agricultural labourers'
strike. On the left of the picture stands
a labourer worn to the bones by "sharp
misery." On the right, an itinerant agitator
of the most truculent contour—no doubt a
very correct portrait of this most terrible
monster; whilst the centre is occupied by a
stout farmer and an aristocratic looking person
with coroneted head, who asks the farmer if
he does not think they can settle the differ-
ences between themselves and the wretched
looking being at their side without the help
of the agitator.
Now it may be said, from whatever side
people look at this question, that facts are
facts, and if anything oonneeted with this
- strike has been borne full and impartial testi-
mony, to it is that this union amongst the
labourers has been a spontaneous thing—that
it !Tread from district to district, and from
one county to another, by its own energy-7-
unprovoked, unforced by any extraneous help.
That men from outside have spoken to these
labourers is true—but it was to advise and
counsel after the movement bad commenced,
and not to excite it before the labourers them-
selves had set it on foot. It is true that
gentlemen at the meetings of various Agri-
cultural Chambers have made this charge
against Outside agitators; but all independ
ent testimony gives point-blank contradiction
to it.

Did it not occur to Mr. Punch's artis,

children will require, if properly fed, 6s.
weekly ; then rent at least Is., and fuel wily
very nearly swallow up the remainder. But
there are yet many things to provide for;
soap and candles, clothes and shoes. When I
reckon up these things in detail, I am always
more and more astonished how labourers
continue to live at all." This. is not a flat-
tering sketch of the condition of our "bold
peasantry." Here is,a statement of Mrs.
WILsniRE, a farm-labourer's wife, with six
children :—" We never know what it is to
get enough to eat; at the end of the meal the
children would always eat more. Of bread
there is never enough, the children are
always asking for more at every meal.
I then say, You don't want your father
to go to prison, do you." Were Mrs. Wir.-
slant: Mrs. Punch, she would very likely
feel pained had At to refuse an extra bit ,of
bread to TOBY, Mr. Punch's favourite dog;
but to have to refuse solicited necessary bread
day after day to six never-satisfied children
must be a difficult thing for a mother, and it
can hardly need external stimulant to alter
the state of things which renders so painful a
duty necessary.
But we may be told that these things are
better now—have altered greatly in the labour-
ers' favour. It would be pleasant to believe
that such was the case. But our industrious
Royal Commissions will by no means permit
us to think so. Another of these, which
pursued its labours in 1867, inquiring into
the condition of women and children and the

"Gang System," tells us tales quite as awful
as those which we have already rel%ted. Young
girls walking sixteen miles each day to and

from their work, children dropping through
sheer fatigue unable to reach their homes, a
morality worse than that of Hottentots;
crowded cottages where to breathe wholesome
air was an impossibility;, swarming bedrooms
without discrimination of age or sex. Let the
curtain be dropped before these, and however
you may deal with the agitators, Mr. Punch,
give us no pictorial representation of them.
The labourer's wages, his treatment, and his
life, as representing the spirit of justice and
humanity in men are simply revolting. Every
condition of his life is lowering and demoralis-
ing. Mr. J. E. WHITE in his reportsays—"The
behaviour and language of gangs are described
as extremely coarse, rough, and even to
strangers, BO much so, that a respectable
person meeting a set of these girls and women

cannot venture to speak, scarcely to look at
them, without the risk of being shocked by
them."

Can the landlords and farmers put an end to
these iniquities? If so, -why do they not at
once set about so necessary a task. Why
Invre they remained quiescent till now ?
Mr. Punch's agitator, with his brutal face,
is not a pleasant looking fellow, but why was
it necessary to call him in—that is presuming
always that he has interfered. If thatunfortu-
nate labourer is as shown in the picture, some-
body must step in and protect him. To be fleeced,
brutalised, beggared, without mercy or pity is
a fate upendurable by any class in England
to-day. And when gentlemen in Agricultural
Chambers retort upon their accusers, and say
that things are as had with certain classes of
town workers, we admit it, and cry "so much
the worse." We know it, we acknowledge it.
And whilst doing so, we feel not only regret
and shame, but an apprehension of danger

and does it not occur to every person who looks
at this cartoon that this query arises, namely,
—lf the farmer and landlord can settle this,
between them, why did they not•eettle it
long before this without the stimulus of agita-
tion of any kind? The starvation the
squalor, and generally wretched condition of
the labourer, is not a matter of to-day. It
has existed any time for the last century—
why was it not looked to before? We need
not go back prior to the Poor taw Reform of
1831, to find out that HODGE has been
neglected and ill-used. We have not been
in the dark on this matter at any time, as
Parliamentary commissions have told us all
about it—without Farmer BROADICRES or
his noble landlord troubling their heads to
make it better; or even without Mr. Punch
arousing himself to any great effort on behalf
of the poor silent sufferer. If the agitator,
oven of the ugly type depictured by Mr.
Punch, set the present movement on foot, then
society owes a debt of gratitude to the agitator,
ill-favoured as he is, and if the poor labourer
adds three or four shillings a week to his
wages, 'and the country gains in security by
an improved relationship between labourer
farmer, and landlord, we have a right to pray
for the agitator who stimulated so. good a
work.

If Air. Punch, or any other well-intentioned
but ill-informed person, desires to understand
the condition of the farm labourer in England
over a series of years, there are ample means
at hand for studying his condition, past and
preaent. A great deal may be picked up by a
perusal of the late Mr. NASSAU SENIOR'S essay
in the Edinburgh Review, July 1845. It would
occupy too much space to quote from this essay,
but if any person wishes to understand how
labour can be degraded, and the laboureer pau-
perised, demoralised, brutalised, let him read
what Mr.- SENIOR has to say on this subject.
Or if Mr. Punch prefer the more ponderous
study of Blue books, let him turn to the Re-
ports of Commissioners and Sub-Commis-
sioners appointed in 1842 to inqtfire into the
employment of women and children in agri-
culture, hi different parts "of England, and he
will find that the condition of things de-
scribed is such that no man with a heart, a
oonseience, or the power of thought in him,
can reflect on without pain, or can tolerate
without shame and confusion of face. Dr.
GREENIIP, of Caine, Wiltshire, says, speaking
of the food of labourers' families in that dis-
trict—" When there is a family, potatoes do,
and must necessarily form the principal food.
Fresh butchers' meat is never bought, the
entrails, or in'ards,' as they are called, of
the numerous swine killed here, form the chief
luxury of those who can afford something
better than bread and potatoes."
What do you think of that, Mr. Punch, as
the condition, not of an individual, or a few
individuals, but of a class of men labouring
daily to. increase the wealth of the richest
country in the world? Or, read this compa-
rison between the paupers and the farm
labourers' condition, drawn by the same
hand :—" In our union, the cost of each indi-
vidual, taking the average of men, women,
and children is is. 6d. weekly for food only.
And buyineby tender, and in large quantity,

we buy at least 10 per cent. cheapor than the
labouring man can. But without considering
this advantage, apply the scale to the poor
man's family. A man, his wife, and two

accusations, or illogical recrimination of the
pictorial or verbal kind. Foreign agents have
not set this movement on foot, nor can any
known agency working from outside stop it.
Justice, long delayed, will hive to be done to
the toilers in our fields. We have been living
in a kind of 'fOol's paradise. The noblemen
and gentlemen with the average £20,000 per
annum have been sitting in the sunlight and
singing the praises of a state of things not
unpleasant to them. Other people are now
beginning to ask for some small share of the
light and warmth. How they, are to be

LLOYD JONES.

LANDLORDS, LABOURERS, AND
FARMERS.
MIL CIIALSTOPTEER, NEVILE has thought pro-
per to point out what he calls some "extra-
ordinary fallacies in a paper signed by ALTEED
A. WaizoN," and I claim the right to
challenge his judgment and to show that the
" fallacies " come from him and not from me.
Mr. NEVILE states that I appear "'to agree
with Professor BEESLY that it is the land-
lords who in the end must make up whatever
increase of pay the labourers may receive, and
that if they did succeed in raising wages it
would have to be at the cost of the farmers
who are least able to bear it, and would in no
way affect the extortionate rents paid to the
landlords." Precisely so; that is what Ido
mean. And now for some of the " facts "
which Mr. NEVILE very properly says "ought
to be the foundation of all argument."
Is it a " fact " that the generality of farmers
are accustomed to "luxurious living, keeping
their hunters, and ride in scarkt coats ?" The
italics are Mr. NEVILE'S own, and if he be
really serious in this statement, and. puts it
forward as one of the "facts," then I say at
once he must make himself better acquainted
with his subject bebre he ventures into print
again, unless ho chooses to have Limself set
down as being onv of "those who know little
or nothing about the matter." That some of ,
the "gentlemen farmers" as they call them-
selves who are fanning on their own land may
"keep their hunters" there can be no doubt.
But that farmers do this generally and hunt
over their lords' estate is so palpably incorrect
and untrue that it would be a mere waste of
time to make any further reply to that.
I claim to be as good, if not a somewhat
better authority than Mr. NEVILE on the con-
dition of the tenant farmers and labourers of
this country. I was horn and roared in the
midst of an agricultural district, and stood at
the tail of the plough, and have taken my
part in the harvest field before I was eighteen
years of age, aud although I have subse-
quently been engaged in other pursuits, I am
in the habit of passing through many of the
principal counties in England and Wales tea
or a dozen times a year, and I know that the
general complaint of tonant4armers is heavy
rents, excessive rates and taxes, and this is
exactly what they have been complaining of
through the public) press, at many of the
meetings which have lately been held.
That, there are hero and thero tenant-
farmers living under considerate land-
lords at. moderato rents and doing well, no
one who knows the agricultural districts will
deny. But these are the exceptions to the
general rule, and whoa Mr. NEVILE tolls us
as another of his "facts" that the labourer

•, 2

would, "be glad to get some of the land at
double the rent row paid for it by some of
the farmers who employ them, one cannot re-
sist being impressed with the belief that any-
one making such a statement must "know
little or nothing about the matter."

Then another of Mr. NEVILE'S "facts" is
"the fact that higher rents usually lead to
higher wages," and goes on to say that "A
man with £5 an acre capital can only pay say,
255. per acre rent, but a tenant with £lO
an acre, can pay 33e. or more by a greater
outlay in cultivation, which increases the de-
mand for labour and so raises wages." All
very well Mr. NEVILE, providing the farmers
could all command £lO an acre, and if they
could whistle it down from the clouds when
they wanted it, but £lO an acre means £5,000
for a, farm of five hundred acres, and I venture
to say that the majority of tenant farmers
would have a struggle to raise 5,000 shillings.
No doubt the "gentlemen farmers" could
manage all this very well, but they just
happen to be the very men whom
the labourers complain of as being
the least willing to pay a fair rate of
wages; and Mr. NEVILE'S "facts" about
, higher rents usually leading to higher
wages," are just about as correct as it would be
to say that the deeper a farmer clips his hand
into his purse to .pay a high rent the more he
will have left to pay for labour. No doubt
both rents and wages in some parts of Scot-
land are somewhat higher than in England;
hut Mr. NRVILE supplies the reason of this
himself, namely, because " their farms are let
on leases." Surely no one who has given the
question anything like due consideration, will
expect the great bulk of English and Welsh
tenant farrn,lrs, who are kept as tenants--
at-will for political purposes, to invest
c ipital in a farm that they may be turned out
of the following year. And to attempt to
deny the truth that as a general rule landlords
let their farms for the highest rent they can
obtain for them, is simply to deny what many
of them would never think of denying theta-
selves, and what everybody knows, and the
public press proves to be, a general complaint
among tenant farmers. In proof of this I
need only refer to the admission made
by Lord RADNOR, in pleading the cause of the
agricultural labourers in his charge to the
Grand Jury at the Wilts Quarter &Salons last
week, in which ho stated that the labourers
bad some claim to participate in the in-
creased prosperity and wealth of the country."
Whereupon the Foreman of the Jury stated
that, "As farmers we fail to recognise the
improvement, and believe that those who
protit by the increased wealth should be the
tirst to pay." Lord RADNOU, like a generous
and truthful landlord, frankly admitted the
justice or the foreman's remarks, and said in
reply, that—" It' the farmers are not so thriving
as they could wish lam sorry for it. I am a
landlord myself, and shall assist my tenants
by meeting them half way in order that the
existing grievance may be remedied." A
Juror—" Thank you my lord. If the other
owners of property would but follow your
example we should get on very well indeed."
But will "the other owners of property"
follow his "lordship's example?" Experience
proves they will do no such thing; hence the
necessity of dealing with the land question—
which is essentially the farmers' and labourers'
question as a whole.

I pointed out that In my opinion the
best way to do this would be to carry out
the STEIN system adopted in Prussia, 'or to
pass a Land Mt for Great Britain similar to
the Irish Land Act; or, better still, by adopting
the prineipal laid down by the," Land Tenure
Reform Association." Mr. NEVILE says this
Association " does not adopt the principle of
nationalising the land." I never said it did.
But it, admits the desirability of landed
estate i being bought up on behalf of the State,
whieh gees partly in that direction, and Mr.
Ny.-vrt.t; admits " the experiment may easily
be tried." But, as " a tax-payer," I altogether
object to." Mr. T4O WE " buying it, or, when
purchased, that Government should have any
control over it, as local management and au-
pervisieu. is the only correct principle. Under
any circumstances, whether the land remain
in the hands of private owners, or be partly

under the control of the State, the tenure and
conditions of occupancy under which it is
held must be altered. so as to enable both
labourers and farmers to become occupiers and
cultivators of the soil, and the sooner this is
done the better, as it would be a vain delusion
to suppose that the present movement among
the labourers will settle down by the advance
of two or three shillings a week.

ALFRED A. WALTON.

Brecon, April 22nd.

AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF RAIL-
WAY SERVANTS,
As I am knovn to your readers as an old
labourer for the Tea Hours Bill and other
enactments for the reduction of the length of
the customary day's work, I feel sure that you
will give me space for a letter on the position
of the railway employes, and the history of
the movement now going on amongst them for
the amelioration of their-condition. .
The wrongs of the class of men who are
employed in this department of labour are not
only cruel to themselves, but dangerous to all
railway travellers. These wrongs consist of
low wages for responsible duties; broken con
tracts, by which the managers evade or neglect
the supply of the clothes agreed to he given
as a part of the remuttelation ; excessive hours
without payment for overtime; and continuous
employment, night and day, on special occa-
sions, producing exhaustion and inefficiency in
the service highly dangerous to the public.
Many attempts have been made from time
to time to induce the railway men to co-ope-
rate, but the labour market king glutted with
men seeking such engagements the railway
men did not dare to move., Even now there
hi' great timidity on the part of many. But by
the munificence of Mr. BASS and the labours
of other gentlemen, advantage has been taken
of the present condition of the labour market
to promote some sort of combination amongst
the railway dm ploy es throughout the kingdom,
and there is a wide-spread desire to form an
effective union under the title of" The Amal-
gamated. Society of Railway Servants."
Unfortunately, however, the facility for
combination in the London district and the
promptness of the men in the metropolis in
putting the Society on a legal basis, has created
some jealousy in the provinces; a jealousy
fostered and encouraged by certain people who
charge the London pen with a desire to elect a
particular gentleman as General Secretary,
whilst the men in the provinces ieem equally
anxious to thrust upon the London men
another gentleman whose character and ante-
cedents are not satisfactory to the Metropolitan
men. The advice given by Mr. Thus, myself,
and others, is—" Unite withoutl reference to
either of these candidates for office, and. then
elect your officers when you have got your
union."
My view, and I believe it to be logi-
cally, as well as practically correct, is
that you cannot make any appeal to univer-
sal suffrage unless there is previously
established and acknowledged a provisional
committee, which shall have the power
of arranging the details of the first delegate
meeting out of which the permanent constitution
may legally arise. It is the duty of the provisional
government to secure the effective expression of
the popular will. With this view, and as a
beginning, I aoceptedithe Executive Council,
formed by the London men, viz, as a provi-
sional government to prepare for the appeal to
the suffrages of the whole of the members.
It was found necessftry, however, to do more
than elect a committee. The appeal to the
members could .not be conducted without
expense. Who was to receive the funds?
The law gave no protection for those funds
unless the Society was enrolled; but the
Society could, not be enrolled without rules and
officers. So these have been elected, and rules
prepared and enrolled as a temporary arrange-
ment, to bring the whole affair into a legal
existence.
Some mistakes have, perhaps, been committed,
but there are none which cannot be remedied
by the delegate meeting proposed to be held in
June next, if arrangements can be com-
pleted by that time. With a view to the
holding of that meeting at which the rules are
to be reyieed,ofAcers electcd,and the constitution

of the Society finally deeided upon, a pro-
gramme has been drawn up by myself and
approved by the general council for the con-
sideration of our country friends. It is not to
be taken as settled, but as an outline for con-
sideration; and I shall be glad to receive any
suggestions thereupon from any persons in-
terested in the subject. It is honestly intended
to reconcile the differences which have been
fostered and encouraged amongst the railway
men. It purposes to give to everyone really
interested in the movement the opportunity of
taking part in the construction of the future
rules and government.

It is as follows :
Proposed Programme of the First General Dele-
gate Meeting of the Amalgamated Society of
Railway Servants.

Issued by the Executive Council of the Society,
provisionally constituted under the Trades Union
Acts, Bte.
1. The decision of the majority of the delegates
shall be accepted as binding upon the minority.
2. The rules which have been registered, and
the Council and Officers who have been elected
pro tem., to be accepted as a provisional govern-
ment, until the Delegate Meeting shall have been
duly constituted, and shall have decided upon
other rules, and shall have elected other persons to
perform the executive duties.
3. At the Delegate Meeting, the alterations in
the rules shall be first discussed; but to prevent
loss of time, no alteration shall be entertained
unless notice thereof has been forwarded to the
General Secretary fourteen days before such
Delegate Meeting; and every proposed alteration
duly authenticated shall be printed in a conve-
nient form, so that each delegate at the meeting
may have a copy, and may see the alterations so
proposed. Every proposed alteration shall be
authenticated as having been approved by the.vote
of the majority of a branch sending a delegate, or
as having been approved by at least ten members
of the Society, where a delegate cannot be sent.
But no alteration can be entertained which is
known to be contrary to the provisions of the
Trades' Union Act, under which the .Society is
registered.
4. All Branches having fifty members, to be en-
titled to send a representative ; Branches exceed-
ing 200, to send two delegates; exceeding 400,
three delegates, and no more.

5. Each delegate to produce a credential, signed
by the Secretary and Chairman of the Branch he
represents—each certificate also to be endorsed by
the General Secretary, that the alleged number of
members in the Branch have been enrolled, and
have Paid the levy towards the expenses of the
meetings of delegates.
6. That to meet the convenience of M. T. Bass,
Esq., and other members of Parliament, sympa-
thising with the movement (whose personal advice
and co-operation it is desired to secure),'the Dele-
gate Meeting shall be held in London, on Monday,
June Ist, and two following days; a public
meeting being held on the evening of Wednesday,
the 3rd, to elicit the sympathy of the public, and
to create public opinion in favour of the move-
ment.
_ _ _

7. That the revision of the rules, and the fun.
damentel constitution of the Society, be the
special business of the first and second days; and
that the third day be devoted to the election of the
new Executive Council, and the appointment of
officers, in accorda'nee with the rules adopted by a
majority of the delegates on the two previous days.
On the third day.sball also be discussed any other
propositions not included in the above, of which at
least fourteen days' notice has been given, so that
such proposition can be printed upon the notices
of motion supplied to each delegate, and be well
considered.

8. That the election of the Executive Council
shall be by ballot, in the following manner: Each
delegate shall deposit, in a box provided for the
purpose, a list of the names of the persons he
desires to be elected; and when all the delegates
shall have voted, four scrutineers shall be ap-
pointed, who shall sum up the votes; those
receiving the highest number of votes being
elected as the Executive Council for the ensuing
year. Any voting paper containing more than the
number of names required, shall be void. As soon
as the scrutineers have made their report (which
shall be vouched as correct by their signatutes),
the chairnian shall read the names of the Arsons
elected to the meeting. The election of such
officers as may be chosen by the Delegate Meeting
shall be conducted in like manner.
9. That the chairman of the Provisional Exe-
cutive Council shall take the chair until the
meeting has been constituted, when, as the first
business, he will resign in fa.vour of any other
chairman who may then be elected by the meet-
ing; and such chairman, so elected by the
meeting on the first day, shall preside until the
election of the Executive Council, when he in turn
shall vacate the chair in favour of the president
or vice-president, if present, or in f tvour of the
chairman of the new Executive Coancil, if he shall
have been chosen before the conclusion- of the
business.

10. That with .a view to secure a fair represen•
tation from all parts of the country, the expenses
of each delegate shall be paid as follows :—Three-
fourths of his travelling expenses and maintenance
during the Code:ewe out of the General Fund,
and one-fourth by the Branch sending such Dele-
gate; and with a view to the cre4ion of such
Cieneral Fund, a levy of per Member
be paid into the hands of the General Treasurer on
or before the 16th day of May; no Member who
has not paid this contribution shall be entit!ed to
Vote in the Election of a Delegate, and no Branch
Which has not paid its levy to the Delegate Ex-
pense Fund on or before the 16th of May, shall

be entitled to send a Delegate. The allowance to
each Delegate to commence from the Ist of June,
and to cover such time as may be necessary for
him to return to the branch he represents; such
allowance to be at the rate of per

day.
11. That it shall be in the power of the Meeting,
of Delegates to expel any Member creating dissen-
sion after such Delegate shall have refused or
neglected to respect the ruling of the Chairman;
such Delegate to have no right to take any part in
the proceedings until he shall be re-admitted by a
vote of the Meeting, and shall have expressed
regret for his conduct.
12. That with the exception of the mover and
seconder of a resolution, each Delegate shall limit
his observations to ten minutes, and that the
mover of such resolution alone shall have the
privilege of reply before the motion is put.
Clause 10th in this proposed programme
will probably require re-construction. It
intended to provide for small branches, and at
a distance, to be put as nearly as possible upon
even terms with larger branches in or near
London, which would have no travelling ex-
penses to pay. The problem to be solved is
how to equalise the burden of the expenses
of the delegate meeting, but at the same time
let eanh branch feel a certain responsibility in
sending a delegate. It would only tend to
foster disunion and to encourage unnecessary
expense, if no limit were placed on the number
of delegates to be sent by each branch; the
expenses to be charged on the general fund
must be known before hand. Thus, supposing
a levy of one shilling a member were decided
upon, and there were ten thousand who wished
to be represented by delegates, and ,who paid
the levy, it is clear that the total sum at the
disposal of the promoters of the delegate meet-
ing would be 10,000 shillings or £5OO. Assum-
ing the conference to last three days, and
allowing for country delegates one day to
come up and another to return, with compensa-
tion for loss of time and extra expenses, it seems
to me that the average expenses of the delegates
including those from branches in London and
district, (whose charges would be compara-
tively very small,) could not be less than
£1 13s. 4d. each, Under the mostr favourable
circumstances therefore, if 10,000 members
joined (and if all other expenses beyond those
of the delegates could be defrayed from the
contributions of honorary members), the
largest number of delegates which could be
paid for would be three hundred. It would be
safer to say two hundred and fifty, or one
delegate to every forty members. If 5,000
members only joined and paid the levy, only
125 delegates could be paid for out of the
General Fund.

I regret to state that this financial necessits
has not been clearly understqpd by some of our
friends, and especially by the Editor of a
journal specially claiming to attend to the
interests of the railway employes, and, who,
having no experience in such matters, has
been encouraging the notion that anyone from
anywhere could come up to this delegate meet-
ing without any authority from anybody and
vote for anything, having his expenses paid by
nobody knows whom. This loose and im-
practicable notion is supposed to be gratify-
ing to 'the provincial men, and therefore
the journal referred to refuses to insert
communications respectfully demonstrating
tfie absurdity of. the position. But I have
faith that they will see the truth of the
matter, and judge for themselves where
the common sense lies. Time is, however,
being wasted in the interval by the misrepre-
sentations and. suppressions of the journal re-
ferred to.

The BEE-HIVE has always been the im-
partial advocate of the interests of the whole
of the working classes, and T feel confident
that it will use its influence to encourage the
union of all the railway employes throughout
the country, without consideration for the
personal interests of any individuals seeking
tht office of General Secretary, or an editorial
chair.

For myself I seek no office or pay of any
kind, and shall retire from the position to
which the London men have done the the
honour to elect me as soon as the Delegate
Meeting has been properly constituted, and
the permanent government has been elected.
Now, as then, and always I shall continue to
labour as I have done all my life, for shorter
hours and better wages for the working
classes.

J. BAXTER LANGLEY.

articles.title: CONTAGIOUS DISEASES BILL.
articles.text:
CONTAGIOUS DISEASES BILL.

MY regret that Mr. CHRISTOPHER NEVILE
should be an opponent of these Acts is tem-
pered by the knowledge that he is at all events
thoroughly reasonable and amenable to argu-
ment. I reiterate that the doctors should be
our chief guides in legislating on matters Of
health and disease, and, in so saying, I have
vo wish to ignore the fact that a good many
are opposed to the Bill, amongst whoni may
possibly be found twa or three men of
eminence; but the vast majority of the faculty
are in favour of it.

There is no occasion for the Government to
"establish brothels," but in my humble
opinion the Government cannot afford to
ignore their existence, as it has done. Pros- ,
titntion is a great fact, which no Government
has been able to subdue. All kinds of rulers
have tried to put it down. Paternal Govern-
ments, like that of the POPE, have rigidly
Suppressed. it, and. have been glad to
allow brothels to spring up again under
the nose of the Vatican. 'While con-
venticles and heresies have been utterly
extinguished in some countries, 'prostitution
has beaten every effort of legislation.
Ought not this to teach:us that no animal
function can be suppressed, and that the
system 'of regulating this function by marriage
under immense difficulties which obtains in our
form of civilisation, is a very imperfect one,
and that this sad social evil must be dealt with
otherwise than by suppression or midnight
meetings, or the ignoring of the worst part of
it—the disease which lurks amongst prosti-
tutes. and poisons society at large?
The popular and feminine notion of a
certain disease, is that it is the direct result
and Consequence of utter profligacy and excess.
The truth is, that it is not the adiisequence of
excess, and that the worst profligates are pre-
cisely those that escape. The villain who pol-
lutes his neighbour's bed, or who deliberately
and diabolically seduces innocent maidens,
is perfectlfsafe from'syphilis. The poor lad
seduced in an unguarded moment by a hardened
prostitute, may be pointed at as a mutilated
and properly punished profligate for the rest
of his life.

I repeat, we cannot ignore prostitution;
but for the sake of innocent people we can
and ought to combat the disease which is
propagated by it. We have foul and horrible
sewers in the midst of our cities; we can-
not suppress them, we cannot ignore them;
then let us try and prevent them breediug
poisons that may injure us.

Mr. CHRISTOPIItt NEVILE asks, "wily are
the wives and children of innocent men to
have part of the bread taken out of their
mouths to protect the wives and children of
guilty profligate men ?" The sentiment em-
bodied in this question is not very humane,
but I would remark that tho wives and Children
of profligate mon are also the children,
grandchildren, and near relatives of innocent
men. No family is safe. A wet nurse may
communicate the disease to her foster-child.
The innocent, chaste daughter of a perfectly
innocent family may marry a youth who may
once have been unchaste, and he, believing
himself well, may infect his wife through his
Offspring. I should scarcely call such a youth
"profligate," and from my professional ex-
perience, and general knowledge as a man of
the world, I fear there are not many men
qualified to throw the first stone at such a one.
We have Government Inspectors of factories
and mines; why should the careful and
prudent be taxed to protect the careless and
wilful?

Much stress has been laid on the liability to
error in apprehending prostitutes. Let the
opponents of this Act make the most of this
liability, and assuredly they have done so,
and still the argument applies to every law.
Any one of us is liable to be hanged by mis-
take, but every human precaution has been
taken, in the ease of this Act especially; and
any error on the part of a policeman is-quickly
remedied long before the "instrumental viola-
tion." All women out alone after dark in our
large.eities are liable to unfortunate mistakes
quite apart from the Contagious Diseases Bill.
Solicitation is punishable in London. Mr.
linvlT,E gives an instance of the facility of
error in this respect; and Dr. rALEY says "it

is. better that nine guilty persons should
escape than one innocent person should
suffer ; " should we, therefore, repeal all regu-
lations for the order of the streets, and allow
shameless prostitutes to "solicit" at every
street corner.?

Mr. NET.= is confident that the ruin of
France "has been, in a great measure, caused
by that very system which Mr. BRUCE is so
anxious to see established in England." As
this "very system" is carried out in Germany,
I have an equal right to assume that the
German victories had their source in the
Contagious Diseases Bills of that country.
_

Mr: NEVILE asserts that " the working
class is the most moral class, in the kingdom."
With the full knowledge that lam addressing the
working class especially in your paper, I assert
my belief that they are not one whit more
virtuous than any other class. For obvious
reasons they are less liable to certain vices—
the result of wealth and idleness—but they are
fully as vicious in other respects as lords and
gentlemen. Depend upon it there is no
virtuous class,
.though there are virtuous and
vicious individuals in all classes.

' I owe you; Mr. EDITOR, special thanks for
inserting in your phper my letters, which
contain opinions which I fear are adverse to
your,own and obnoxious to many of your
readers.

articles.title: HUMPITIIEY SA.NDWITH.
articles.text:
HUMPITIIEY SA.NDWITH.

ONE LAW FOR THE RICH AND
ANOTHER FOR THE POOR.
YOUR readers are doubtless well acquainted
with the story of Lady. Twlss, which was
recently before the public; but perhaps few
are acquainted with a peculiar sequel to that
story. I allude to a Bill which, owing to what
occurred in that case, has been. introduced
into Parliament, the fourth clause of which
enacts that '!.whoover shall accuse, or threaten
to accuse, any woman of unchastity with a
view to extort money or other valuable thing,
shall be guilty of felony, and may be subjected
to 'penal servitude for life, or not less than
three years, or imprisonment with hard labour
and whipping." It is not my purpose to com-
ment at all upon this proposed enactment, as
to whether it would be a bad or good enact-
ment. But my purpose in writing to you is to
point out the very different view which Par-

Lament takes of an acousation brought against

the chastity of a rich woman and a similar
accusation brought against the chastity of a
poor woman. We who oppose the Contagious
Diseases Acts, have kept bringing before these
gentlemen the fact that, under the operation
of these Acts, men are actually paid by the
Government—Metropolitan policemen in plain
clothes—to accuse women.of unehastity ; and
we have brought forward the danger resulting
to poor women from such a system. To this
we have continually received the answer—.
,4 These men will very seldom mistake; they
will never accuse anyone of unchastity who is
not% prostitute; and, if they do, she can easily
prove that she is a chaste woman; she
has only to call a few witnesses, and
can easily rebut the charge." Now, Sir,
we know what all that is worth; we know
that these ads make it a much more difficult
thing for a woman falsely accused to escape
from their fangs than such a statement as this
would seem to suppose. But that is not the
point which I have to deal with. What we
have all along said is this, "However easy a
thing it may be for a woman falsely accused
to prove that she is not a prostitute, and thus
to escape frorq the fangs of this law—how-
ever easy or difficult that may be—it is a
grievous and intolerable thing to expose, by
express Government enactment, our poorer
women to the accusation of unchastity. The
very accusation in itself brings blight on a
woman's character and is a means of ruining
her.'' Nay more, we say that in the conditions
of our society, there are not a few instances in
which some slip from virtue may have been
long ago repented of and atoned for, and it is
a terrible thing for a woman that it should be
in the power of paid Government officials, any
day they like, by bringing a careless or
malicious accusation against her, to compel
her whole previous life to be laid bare before
the public. And we said to these rich men
, how would you like if it was in the hands of a

set of spies any day to bring your whole
previous life before the public? And yet such
an accusation against a man is, owing
to the present mischievous inequality of
the social standard, a very light thing
for him to bear in comparison with what it
is for a woman to bear. Some few mera-
hers of Parliament doubtless have felt
these arguments; many more have been
obliged to listen to them by their constituents.
But it was not till the matter was ringing
through the country that Parliament took any
action in it, and it was not until demands for
Repeal had been brought to bear upon them
throughout the length and breadth of the land
that we heard of any movement in Parliament
about the matter at all. And why is it, Sir,
that it was so? Why did they require such
pressure before they took up the question? It
was because it was the poor who were affected,
and not the rich. It would have been another
story if it had been the rich who were affected.
For let us turn now to tills case of Lady Twiss.
Here is a rich lady, the wife of a man moving
in what they call "good society ;" an accusa-
tion of unchastity is brought against her, it
ruins her; and Parliament at once feels the
gravity of the case; "society," as they call it,
has received a shock. They quickly find out
now that it is a monstrous thing indeed that a
woman should be exposed to such accusations,"
and in a week's time we find that Parliament,
by its spontaneous action, has produced a Bill
on the subject. The comparison of the dealing
of Parliament with these two cases is indeed
very instructive. The present Parliament,
Sir, is one which represents the rich,
and not the poor. It is a Parliament
which deals very, harshly, very blunderingly,
and very ignorantly, with the case of the poor.
It seems to see in the poor only persons for
whom penalties are to be multiplied, and new
police regulations put in force. I think,
indeed, it may truly be said that the present
House of Commons, as a body—theee are in-
deed some noble exceptions, but they are very
few and far between—knows nothing of the
poor. And, indeed, a very grave question for
this country just now lies in this gross and
culpable ignorance, which we find with respect
to the poor, and especially with respect to poor
women, among those who are our legislators
If ever they do legislate properly for the poor,
it is because the matter is forced upon them
from without. It is not because they
sympathise with the case and know how to
deal with it. There is no easy and nataral
sympathy in their hearts with the poor. Ignor-
ance of the poor is bred in their, very bones.
And what is this owing to? It is owing, I
suspect, chiefly to these grievous class distinc-
tions which exist, to those strong lines of
demarcation which out off one end of society

from the other—class distinctions which the
blundering ignorance of our legislators tends
continually to widen. This class distinction
must become mollified or intensified, and the
future of our nation depends on the result.
The way in which this class distinction
is to be obliterated, I firmly believe, is
by sowing the seeds of. institutions
and laws, containing in themselves

the princhles of their own oontinuance, and
which.are such as to work against class dis-
tinction. Such institutions of such laws will
never arise from a legislature ignorant of the
poor, but can only arise from a legislature
which contains in it strong sympathies for all
classes of the country. Let us look to it then
that when the next generaliveleetion comes.
men are returned to Parliament who have in
them some living heart of sympathy for the
poor as well as for the rich, and who feel that
an injury<lone to even the meanest subject is
an injury done to the whole commonwealth

just as truly as if the injured person were one
of high estate. A one-sided legislature can
only create one-sided measures; and these
pave the way for confusion and trouble. It is
our duty to ourselves and to our posterity, our
duty to the future of the great country of
which we are all citizens, to see that in the
next Parliament there is a strong admixture
of all those elements which can best represent
the poor,

JAMES STILLET,
Fellow and Assistant Tutor of
Trinity College, Cambridge.:

QUESTIONS BY A POSITIVISr.
ELEVENTH QUESTION.—Was OWEN a scion-
tub o man,? Was he or his system accepted as
scientific by any leading thinkers of the day,
past or present? Was not COMTE a scientific

man? Is not his system founded on vientifio
principles? And has not this fact been
admitted by eminent scientific thinkers, past
and, present, and is not his system growtng in
reputation and spreading? Can his system
be understood unless his " Philosophy," his
"Polity," and his "Catechism" have been
read and studied?

ANSWER.—OWE N had but little knowledge
of the ordinary sciences, it is true. But he had
acquired, in the most practical manner, the
only knowledge or science which can make a
competent social reformer—the knowledge of

he Causes of evil and of good to man. Edu-

cation under the guidance of this knowledge
is the only basis upon which an effective system

of social reform n can be constructed. And I have

never met with any other writer on education
who has not shown most plainly in his writings
(to any one possessing the information news-

sary for forming an intelligent opinioti on the
subject) the absence of this indispensable
knowledge, by which alone education can be
made a scientific process for the forming of a

really good intellectual and moral character.
But although Mr. OWEN had acquired this

knowledge, and had verified it piut;tieally in
the most oonolusive manner, and although
he devoted his life for more than forty

years to endeavour to explain it, ha
could not make the subject understood. 1
must here repeat that the truth upon which
the science of education is based (Lira man is
the creature of causation) is a truth of mental

science. And this branch of knowledge (very

easily understood when rightly pointed out) was

se extremely imperfect, that this truth could
not be explained and was supposed to be at
variance with another highly important truth
(that man has a power of self-government),
which, of course, could not without error be
denied, and which it is, in various ways, very
injurious to deny, but which was denied by
Mr. OWEN. And the consequence was, that
his statements upon this subject were so

extremely confused (just as we find at this •
day the statements of Mr. Mut, Mr. lIERnEwr
SPENCER, Mr. BAIN, and others upon the
same aubject on the one hand, and those of
all who write in favour of free will—Sir
WILLIAM HAMILTON, Professor MANSEL, &O.
—on the other) that the "eminent thinkers"
who endeavoured to understand Mr. OWEN'S
explanations of the practical application of
his fundamental truth in education, could not
understand him. And, judging without the
knowledge by which alone they could be enabled
to form an intelligent opinion upon the subject,
they put aside his writings with the idea that
their own thoughts were much in advance of -
those which he endeavoured to propound. But
the truth was, not that these " thinkers " were
wiser than Mr. Ownr, as they imagined tliey
were, but that they were note sufficiently
advanced to be able to understand the true -
parts of his views and their immense import-
ance. They were sufficiently advanced to be
able to see that there were errors in Ws
writings, or that there was much in them which
did not agree with their own previously formed
opinions ; but they could not under-
stand the means, as he described them, by
which every fairly-organised child may be -
caused to acquire a character immensely
superior, intellectually and morally, to any
which has hitherto been known. They mis-
took their own ignorance and false ideas upon
this subject for superior knowledge, and
imagined that Mr. OWEN'S views,
whore
they were eminently practical and matter
of fact, were erroneous and visionary.
th

An attempt was made by several eminent
men—by Lord. Buananku, the Marquis of
LA.NSDOWNE, and others—Who had seen with
admiration the effects which Mr.. OWE N pro-
duced in the ohildren of his work-people, to
copy the New Lanark system of education.
But the Infant School which they establiihed
in Westminster was never any representation
of the original school at New Lanark. And in
all the progeny of Infant Schools which has
since appeared, there has never been anything
resembling tile original "Institution for the

Forination of Character." If these gentlemen
had understood the subject they would never
have imagined that schools can be formed in
the present state of society in which a really
good education can be given to the young I
oven by wasters and mistresses possessing the
necessary knowledge and enlightened goodness.
And there are no such masters and mistresses.
And there never can be any until men and
women have acquired the knowledge of the
causes of evil and of good in the formation of
character, fko. So long as children are
influenced continually by the ideas, and feel-
ings, and practices, and general arrangements
of the present system, there can never be any
approach to a really good education. Even
the exceptional influences which Mr. OWEN
" was able to combine at New Lanark were very
imperfect. We must have our new co-opera-
tive villages, organised in aocordanoe with the
knowledge and spirit of the new system, and
we must have educators who have acquired
this knowledge and spirit, and we must have
parents and others to influence the children
from birth, who are themselves under the
influence of this knowledge and spirit, before
we can have even the first elements of the
means which are necessary to educate the
young as they ought to be educated.
What then can be the value of the opinions
upon this subject of the "men of science or
eminent thinkers" of the old 'world? The
knowledge of all the ordinary sciences united
will not enable men to form an intelligent
opinion in reference to a new science of which
they do not know even the first rudiments.
It matters not that M. COMTE was a scientific
man, and that his system was founded upon
scientific principles. It is evident in his
writings that the sciences with which he was
conversant, and the scientific principles upon
which his system is founded, do not include
the knowledge which alone can form the basis
of an effeotive system of social reform. Nor
has this knowledge been acquired by the
eminent scientific) thinkers who "admit that
his system is founded on scientific principles,"
or by the public with whom it is "growing in
reputation." And it is not by reading and
studying the works of M. COMTE, or by under-
•standing his system, that the ability to judge
intelligently the true principles of social re-
form, can be acquired. It is only by obtaining
the knowledge of the causes of evil and of
good to man.

No one can know the disciples of M. COMTE
without having the highest respect for their
intellectual and moral attainments; but it
cannot be doubted by any one who knows the
intellectual and moral attainments which are
necessary for tho construction of a social
system of true enlightenment and enlightened
goodness, tbdt they have much to learn before
they can judge correctly between the views of
Mr. ()FEN and those of M. COMTE. When
they are able to do so, I Imo no doubt as to
what their judgment will be. And the step
will 'not bo difficult for men who are so far in
advance of nvipy of the prejudices of thpught
nod feeling of which the public opinion of the
old immoral world is composed. They are
educating provisionally a very valuable part
of the human material which is wanted for the
construction of a social system of true en-
lightenment and enlightened goodness. But
the education which is wanted may be effected ,
much more directly and easily, 'and in fact
it can only be effected, by going at once
to the higher department of knowledge to
which as yet they are strangers. It will be of
great importance to have men and women
who have acquired the good and valuable
parts of the culture of what is called civilisa-
tion, but who have thrown off the injurious
and absurd parts of it, to assist the working
classes in the practical commencement, and in
the development, of the mental and material
regeneration of the world. And Positivism will
do much towards the elimination of what is
bad or injurious. But there is much to be
eliminated from Positivism, which only the
knowledge of the causes of evil and of good to
man can remove.

It is most encouraging to know that this
knowledge is now _sufficiently prepared for
practical application. And being so prepared,
it will now be easily acquired by every intelli-
gent pets= who will try to acquire it, And

lit may be acquired sufficiently for general
practical purposes without the laborious pre-
paration which is deemed by our Positivist
friends to be necessary for the study of their
system. And when the necessary knowledge
has been obtained by individuals, the en-
lightened goodness which this knowledge alone
can enable them to acquire may be attained
without much difficulty by those who have
not been too much deteriorated by the influ-
ences of the old. world, if they will study to
regulate their social feelings by its guidance.
If earnest men could know by anticipation the
immensely beneficial results and the highly
pleasurable satisfaction which will proceed
from this knowledge, it would become to them
the first great absorbing subject of study and
contemplation. And they would no longer
imagine that the knowledge of the ordinary
sciences, or any other of the mental acquire-
ments which are now held in high estimation,
can make a man really enlightened. Let me
repeat, that no one can.be really enlightened
who is ignorant of the causes of evil and of
good to man in the formation of character, &c.
HENRY TRAMS.

articles.title: WORKING MEN'S LORD'S DIY REST ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S LORD'S DIY REST
ASSOCIATION.

On Tuesday evening the fifteenth annual
meeting of the members and friends of this
association was held in Exeter Hall, under the
presidency of the Earl of Shaftesbury. The
attendance was numerous, the large hall being
more than three-parts full.
Mr. Charles Hill, the secretary, read an
abstract of the report, wl)ioh made special
reference to the recommendations of the Com-
mission on the Sunday employment of rural
postmen and announced that Mr. Charles
Reed, M.P., to whom the association was so
much indebted, intended to ask the Government
whether these recommendations would be
carried out. Speaking of the Act of Charles
11., the report confessed that there might be
room for amendment, but it ought not to be
repealed, and the association would continue to
resist all attempts in that direction. To
counteract the evil of Sunday excursions the
committee proposed to make similar cheap
outings on Mondays' and they doubted not
the experiment would be attended with success.
The abolition of six-day cab lioences had led
to an increase of Sunday cabs. The under-
takers, of whom 4,000 were kept at work on
Sundays, with the help pf the committee, were
struggling for a free Sunday, while similar
support was being given to railway servants
in their endeavours to lessen their Sunday
work. During the winter 105 lectures were
delivered to 22,000 persons under the auspices
of the association; 8,500 publications had
been issued, and 150,000 were now in prepara-
tion. The receipts amounted to £BlO, and the
expenditure to 1,685.
The chairman, in expressing satisfaction
with the report, mentioned that he had re-
ceived a telegram from Air. Charles Reed,
who was detained in the House of Commons,
intimating that the Government would give
facilities to the letter-carriers to free them-
selves from Sunday labour; but the noble lord
added his conviction that to make the relief
effective the Legislature must prohibit the
delivery of letters on Sundays at post-offices,
otherwise when one postman Was released a
dozen persons would be employed to fetch the
letters. He referred to his Glasgow visit as
affording him evidence of the love and venera-
tion Scotch working men felt for the Sabbath,
not a fanatical but a hearty and sincere and
calm sympathy with the origin and object of
the sacred institution, and he rejoiced to
observe that a similar feeling was spreading
largely amongst the youth of the metropolis.
The report was adopted on the motion of
Mr. Dickson, seconded by the Rev. J. C.
Jones, the resolution also affirming that the
people were opposed to the opening of the
British Museum on Sundays.
Dr. G. H. Davis moved a resolution
approving of Oa recomMendations of the
recent Commission, and regretting that some
substantial relief was not proposed for postmen
in towns as well, which was seconded by Mr.
H. Varley, and carried by acclamation.
A vote of thanks was afterwards passed to
the chairman, and the meetin,g which opened
with prayer, closed with a hymn.

LONDON.
THREATENED STRIKE IN THE ORGAN BUILDING
TRADE.

A second meeting of the employes in the above
trade was held on Wednesday night at Lawson's
Rooms, Gower-street, to take into consideration
the reply of the masters to a petition formed of
certain resolutions passed at a former meeting
with reference to the present hours of labour.
The chair was taken by Mr. F. Tomkins, M.A.,
LL.D., and upon the platform were several in-
fluential gentlemen and members of the musical
profession.
The demand of the men is that the hours of
labour shall be reduced from 60 to 54 per week,
with a half holiday on Saturday. The reply agreed
upon at a meeting of the masters is to the effect
that the nine hours system will be conceded, but
that it will be accompanied by a forfeiture of
certain privileges hitherto enjoyed by the men,
and making other arbitrary conditions.
After delegates from different firms of employers
had read their report, several resolutions were put
to the meeting, and carried unanimously. The.
first was to the effect that the( proposals of the
employers cold not be accepted; the second,
that the meeting viewed with the deepest regret
the course taken by Messrs. Gray and Davison, in
discharging the *delegates sent to them by the
working men, and approving of the conduct of
their fellow-workmen in upholding-them ; and a
third, recommending the, employes of Messrs. Gray
and Davison to stand'out, and pledging the meet-
ing to supply funds to support the discharged
workmen.
The meeting was very enthusiastic, and a
very strong feeling was manifested against some of
the masters who have made themselves obnoxious
to the men. It was stated that a similar move-
ment is in progress in Manchester, Liverpool,
Leeds, Sheffield, and several of our larger towns,
and steps are being taken to consolidate the union
more effectually.

BOLTON.
TILE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF MINERS.

Mr. 'l'. Halliday, president of the Amalgamated
Association of Minors, addressed a meeting of
working men in the Co-operative Hall, Bolfon, on
Monday evening. Afterwards resolutions wore
passed pledging the meeting "to do all in its
power to aid in getting prohibited by law the
working of women and young persons for more
than 54 hours per week," and " to assist in getting
the Criminal Threats Act either repealed or so
amended as not to bear arbitrarily against the
interests of the trade unionists of the country."
The meeting also "hoped that the Government
would pass the Mines Regulation Bill without
its being injured in any material point, and it also
hoped that the Masters' and Servants' Wages
Bill would also pass.

BURNLEY.
STRIKE OF MOULDERS.

In consequence of a refusal to advance wages
from 325.
,to 3s. per week, the moulders have

Messrs. Whittaker and Lupton's, Bracewell an

articles.title: DUN DM.
articles.text:
DUN DM.

DOMESTIC SERVANTS AND THEIR GRIEVANCES.

On Friday night a meeting of domestic servants
resident in Dundee and neighbourhood was held.
There was a numerous attendance, the room being
quite fall. The Dundee Advertiser says :—" Two
girls addressed the meeting at some length, con.
tending that the domestia servants were entitled to
have a half holiday weekly and a free Sabbath
every fortnight. They stated that thoy saw
nothing to prevent such an arrangement being
carried out; but, if there really was anything to
prevent all the servants getting away on one day,
a full holiday mice a fortnight might be substituted.
Then it was considered that if the servants got up
at six o'clock in the morning
.and went to bed at
ton, there would be sufficient time to do all the
work required of them ; while it was strongly
argued that no labour should be performed on
Sunday except what was absolutely necessary. It
was declirad that on Sabbath there was usually
special cooking, and that hence a great amount of
labour was entailed on the servants, which they
did not experience on the other days of the week;
and that Sabbath, therefore, entailed an amOunt
of drudgery which was unbearable. A long and
animated discussion afterwards took place as to
the restrictions which were placed upon the wear-

ing apparel of the servants. It was contended
that if they were compelled to wear what was
generally know* as a " flag " it should be at the
expense of the mistress. The opinion was, how-
ever, that it ought not to be worn at all. The
stipulations as to what should be worn in the way
of dress and jewellery were also considered, and it
was thought the mistress had no right to interfere
with their wearing apparel in any way so long as
it was paid for. Some humorous remarks were •
made as to the' stringency with whii mistresses
ingeired into the chatacter :of their servants. It
was pointed out that they were perfectly omnipo-
tent in their control of their servants' career, and
it was urged that it was high time that the
domestic servants should form themselves into an
organisation, whereby they would be enabled to
secure information not only regarding the °ha--
meters of those who -might become their em-
ployers, but also respecting their general temper
and conduct. It was agreed to form an assooia,-.
tion."

articles.title: LANCASHIRE.
articles.text:
LANCASHIRE.

THE COTTON TRADE.

Mr. Mundella's Nine Hours Bill was among the
subjects discussed at the meeting of the Manchester
Chamber of Commerce on Monday. Mr. Hugh
Mason, who presided, objected to the measure as at
once wrong in principle and singularly ill-timed.
In his opinion the question of the hours of labour
"ought to be left to the operation of those natural
,laws which had already done so much to benefit
men, women, and children working in factories."
If the Bill passed, it would seriously interfere
with the cotton industry, whieh at the present
moment was in no condition to stand experiments
of this kind. The outlook for Lancashire was not
a cheering one. In many districts factories had
been partially stopped, while profits had "entirely
disappeared." Ho looked forward to "very con-
siderable distre.3s," and to "bankruptcies and
compositions." Mr. It. Haworth and Mr. E.
Waltusley, of Stockport, spoke to the same (Afoot ;
and it wits decided 'slat the speeches of the three

gentlemen we have named should be printed and
distributed among the members of the House of
Commons.

•
NEWCASTLE.
°PERUKE rg Tau ENGINEERING TRADE;

A meeting called by the Nine flours League,
which represents the engineering workmen of
Newcastle and Gateshead, was held at Newcastle
on Monday to discuss the present system of over-
time whereby men must work 54 hours up before
overtime counts. There was a small attendance.
The speakers argued that the present system was
unjust to steady workmen, and that it savoured of
niggardliness on the part of employers. Each day's
work ought to stand for itself. Systematic over-
time was denounced, and the meeting adopted a
resolution desiring an amendment in the present
system. It was also resolved to send delegates
from each shop to take further steps in promoting
the alteration.

GLASGOW.
TUE MINES REGULATION RILL.

At a numerously-attended meeting of Scotch
mine-owners, held at Glasgow on Friday, it was
reported that the Home Secretary had, declined to
carry out the amendment in the Mines Regulation
Bill agreed upon at the conference between the
mine-owners and the miners' delegates. The
meeting resolved to petition against the objection-
able clauses in the Bill. In the petition agreed
Upon objection is takento the introduction into the
Bill of clauses affecting education, unless in the
ease of young boys, and to exceptional legislation
affecting merely commercial questions, such as
payment of wages, which should be proided for
in.the general legislation for the country. The
petitioners also complained of clauses which will
make owners, agents, and managers liable for

offences committed by workmen, and of examina-

control of the Home Secretary in place of a board
of examiners eleated for the purpose in the manner
provided in the Merchant Shipping Acts; and they
further object to certain general rules of such an
inflexible character as to render mine-owners
responsible for matters truly beyond their control.

LEEDS.

THE DISPUTE IN TILE FLAX TRADE.-DEMON-.
STRATION IN RoNouu or A RELEASED PRISONER.

It may be remembered that about a fortnight
ago an elderly woman named Newsome, living in
Holbeck, was sent to Armley Gaol for fourteen
days, by Mr. Blum, for intimidation in connection
with the flax strike. ller term of imprisonment
expired on Saturday morning, and she was
liberated. It was determined by the flax operatives
and others that there should be a demonstration
expressive of sympathy with her; but as the
morning was deemed an inconvenient time to do
this effectually, it was decided that it should be
deferred till the evening. Accordingly, shortly
after six o'elock in the evening, a procession started
from the Assembly Rooms, Crown-street, bound
for Armloy. It was headed by Mr. Kendall, the
chairman, and other members of the Flax Opera-
tives' Committee, and was accompanied by the
Leeds Model Band. Considerable excitement was
occasioned along the route, and many dequisitions
were made to the procession till, on getting into
Armley-road, it had assumed very large pro-
portions. The woman Newsome was staying at
the Oak Inn, Armley-road, having been brought
thence in a cab amidst tremendous cheering and
other demonstrations. The cab having been con-
verted into an open carriage so that the released
prisoner might be seen by all on the route, the pro-
cession returned. Mrs. Newsome lives in Baines-
street, Holbeck, near Messrs. Marshall's mills, and
her home was reached by way of Now Wortley.
On arrival at the house, the crowd by that time
having become very large, Mr. Kendall made a
short speech, which was inaudible to alrexcept
those just under him. The gathering soon after-
wards dispersed, having behaved throughout in an
orderly manner. In connection with the dispute
we may state that the Committee give out that
there are 8611 1,100 operatives, chiefly girls, on
the books as out on strike and to pay ; whilst on
the other hand it is affirmed that Messrs.
Marshall's work-people are daily returning on the
terms agreed upon.

articles.title: SOUTH WALES. COLLIERS' WAGES.
articles.text:
SOUTH WALES.
COLLIERS' WAGES.

An important delegate meeting has been held at
Pontypridd. 120 delegates wore present, repre-
senting upwards of 30,000 colliers., It was resolved
that the Executive Committee of the Union should
be asked permission to servo the house-coal masters
of Glatuorganshire with one month's notice for not
having given the 2d. por ton advance asked for on
the Ist of April. It was also agreed that the
improved trade of the district warranted an addi-
tional 10 per cent. rise being applied for, and that
an invitation be given to the steam-coal masters
to meet a deputation of the men at Cardiff to
discuss the question. The meeting pledged itself
to do all in its power to carry out the resolution of
the St. Helens' Conference to commence the eight-
hour system on the Ist day of July next.

Carpet Weavers' Association was held on Saturday

IMMINENT STRIKE IN TUE HOSIERY TRADE.

A conference has just taken place between the
framework knitters of Nottingh.tm, .Arnol,l, and
other places, and the hosiery manufacturers, on
the subject of a revised list of prices, and the pro-
posed abolition of the systena of frame rents. The
men submitted that the reductions made by the

masters for rent of frames, oiling, standing,
winding, and other items brought their average
earnings really down to 12s. 3d. per week; that
those reductions were not made either in the silk
or other trades, and that the deduction was an in-
justice which rendered the trade, so far as the
workmen were concerned, worse than the ,employ-
=tit of farm labourers, and an exorbitant profit
received by the employers which was enjoyed by
capitalists in no other trade. The hosiers submit-
ted a net list of prices recognising a fair remuner-
ation to the owners of machinery, but abolishing
the present system of frame rents. The men have
given the employers an ultimatum extending to
seven days, when they intend to come out on
strike if the concession should not be granted.

articles.title: HUDDERSFIELD.
articles.text:
HUDDERSFIELD.

MR. MUNDELLA AND TIIE OVERTIME SYSTEM.

On Friday evening a large and enthusiastic
meeting of operatives was held at Huddersfield to
take into consideration the question of overtime in
factories. It was explained that the system of
overtime had prevailed to such an extent in the
woollen manufactures that if some action were not
promptly taken a panic would inevitably ensue;
and it was stated that what the operatives wanted
was to "lay away " at six o'clock regularly.

The Chairman read the following letter from
Mr. Mundella, M.P. for Sheffield :
"House of Commons, April 17, 1872.

" 3.1" v DEAR llrra,—The factory operatives in
your neighbourhood have in a letter to me ex-
pressed their desire for legislative interference to
pre vent the working of overtime. The only per-
sons under the existing acts of Parliament who
can work overtime in factories are adult males,
and the Legislature will not, and in ray opinion
ought not, to attempt to regulate the hours of
labour of men. If the working hours are exces-
sive, the remedy is in their own hands. Surely
the men employed in the factories of Yorkshire
can do for themselves what has been done by the
artisans in the majority of trades. I would earnestly
warn the working men against investing this
House with the power of dealing with their hours
of labour. The poor man's labour is his capital,
and Government has no right ta limit or control
him in the use of it. Let them retain this power
in their own hands, and rely upon their own
efforts to obtain fair rates of wages and reasonable
working hours.—Always faithfully yours,

"A. J. MUNDELLA."

Mr. B. Manes moved a resolution to the effect
that it was desirable the system of overtime should
ho bbeished.

Mr. E. Armitage seconded and Mr. W. Brooke

(two extensive manufacturers) and Mr. J C. first
(representing another extensive firm) supported
the resolution, which was passed.
Mr. Jepson moved a resolution, to the
effect that overtime was a great evil, and that all
should be done that could be done to put a stop to
it. It was seconded by Mr. W. Shaw (mmulac-
turer), and carried.

NOTTINGHAM-.
END OF TIIE TAILORS' STRIVE.

On Saturday, a largely attended meeting of the
men on strike in connection with the Nottingham
Tailors' Association was held at the George and
Dragon Inn, Nottingham, when the result of the
conference between their late
.employers and the
representatives of the men were announced. Mr.
Peter Shorrocks, Secretary of the Amalgamation,
was in attendance, as was also Mr. Bailey, the
President ; and they were introduced by Mr,
Tebb, president of the Nottingham branch, and
were loudly cheered by the men.
Mr. Peter Shorrocks said he was pleased to find
that the particulars of the now log had been sub-
mitted to the men, and that they bad placed that
amount of confidence in the Committee which they
so well deserved. He had been on similar com-
mittees for some years past, and was well aware of
the arduous labours attending them, as well as the
amount of feeling with which they had to contend.
It was by no means an enviable position for any
man to be placed in; for, after they had left
room where there had been some degree of bicker-
ing with the masters, they bad to go before the
men, often with less spirit, and sometimes to ob-
serve a great deal more acrimonious spirit. lie
wished to impress upon them the fact, that though
perhaps every one of them might not, when they
came to work by the log, find it to be equal to
what they had expected, yet it was a great advance
which they had obtained. First of all, they had
obtained an advance on their rate per hour of 11 I
per cent. That was. a great step. Then, as to the
log, they had obtained a concession, which brought
the whole advance up to about 20 per cent. That,
be repeated, was a great step indeed. It was equal
to an average increase of 48. upon every pound
they earned, and this would cover most of their
rents during tho week. These wore raAtters worth

5 *

looking at; and when they knew that by their
unity, which had come into very recent existence,
this result had been obtained, they ought to keep
to that unity, and show the country that they were
deserving of the confidence of the executive when
it was given to the tailoring Arad° of Nottingham
to carry out4he present movement:

Mr. Bailey, President of the Amalgamation, ex-
pressed his hope that the tailors of Nottingham
would not disgrace themselves in the eyes of other
trades who, though they bad never seen or known
them, had afforded them liberal pecuniary and
moral support. By all means, let them stick to
what they believed was right.

LIVERPOOL.
TIM TAILORS.

The tailors of Liverpool have sent the following
circular to their employers :

GmsrrLETuEN,—W-e solicit your attention to a
question which has for some time been under the
consideration of the operative tailors of Liverpool,
that is of seeking an advance in our rate of wages,
in order that they may be more consistent with the
improved position of other branches of industry,
and that we, as a trade, may share in the present
general advancement and prosperity.
We respectfully submit, that whilst there has
been a general and gradual increase in the mone-
tary value of the neeessarie I of life and the
domestic requirements so necessary to home re-
sponsibilities and comforts ; and that whilst almost
all other grades of artisans and labourers have
made rapid strides in improving their social posi-
tion, both in advance of wages and reduction of
hours of labour, we as a class remain, for the
most part, in a most unenviable situatiori—worL-
ing longer hours, at an indifferent rate of pay, to
meet the increasing demands against us, unt I
exhausted and unable to meet the oxigenci6s cf
life, and feeling acutely our degradation, we are
constrained to consider our position.

Therefore a special general meeting of the trade
was held in the Concert Hall, Lord Nelson-street,
having regard to these matters at which it was
unanimously resolved—

"That in the opinion of the journeymen tailors
of Liverpool, the time has arrived when an advance
of one halfpenny per hour on the rate of wages is
essentially necessary to enable us as workmen to
meet the legitimate demands of our position; and
although wo are convinced that the 'lo4 ' or time
list' under which we at present work, is unfair in
its construction and unsatisfactory in its working,
yet we trust that at some future time it will be
revised by masters and men duly appointed for the
purpose."

TIVES.

ployers in the felt tiade is now at an end, the

THE BUILDING TRADES.

A deputation appointed by the building opera-
tives has been received by the representatives of
the Builder' Association. The deputation said
they wished to know whether the masters would
accede to fifty-four hours, 80 as to employ the men
summer and winter. They also wanted an increase

MINCIIESTER.
THE OPERATIVE BAKERS AND THE SHORT TINIE

MOVEMENT.

On Tuesday a meeting of operative bakers was
held in the Memorial Ilall, Alhort-squaro, under
the auspices of the Manchester and Salford Trades
Council, for the purpose of advotatiog fewer hours

of labour. Mr. C. Stewart occupied the chair,
and there was a numerous attendance.
Mr. T. Fairbrothez- said they had met to
ascertain whether they were prepared to carry out
the reso'ution which had been submitted to their
employers. They had tried by committee and other
means to 'brill% the matter to a successfnl issue as
between themselves and their employers, but they
could get no further with it, and they found they
wonld have to make a stand one way or the other.
The question was whether they were prepared to
make that stand to place themselves on a footing
with other trades. They were net asking for 54
hours a week; they were only asking for 60
hours per week, or an hour a day longer than any
other trade worked. They were willing to give
twelve o'clock starts on Monday and Friday morn-
ings, and three o'clock starts on the other four
days, and they asked an increase of 28. per week
in wages. The question was whether they would
support that demand or let the movement cease.
The meeting was also addressed by Mr. J.
Bedale and Mr. T. H. Bedale ; after which Mr.
W. IL Wood moved :—" That this meeting is of
opinion that the claims of the operative bakers for
the reduction of the working hours to 60 per week
and an advance of 2s. per week is just and reason-
able, and respectfully urges upon the employers of
