Mr. Ballard (bookbinder) seconded the motion,
which was passed.
Mr. Hodson moved a resolution to the effect
that in the event of the employers declining to
concede their demands notice should be given on
the 4th of May to terminate on the 11th. Mr. J.
Leech seconded the motion, which was passed. A
baker asked if all the men were to come out if one
employer conceded the demands and another did
not. Mr. Fairbrother said the matter was not a
public one at all, but a question to be discussed
and decided among themselves at their club-
houses.

OLDHAM.
TIIII DEMONSTILA.TION COIL ITTEE.

On Wednesday evening last, delegates from the
various trade societies that took part in the public
demonstration on Saturday, April 13th, met in
committee at the Bath hotel, to wind up their
proceedings.
After a balance sheet had been submitted and
adopted, the following resolution was unanimously
carried :—" Tbat this committee, consisting of
representatives from the various trades societies,
that took part in the demonstration on Saturday,
April 13, hereby respectfully tenders its best thanks
to his worship the Mayor of Oldham (A. Crompton,
Esq.), for the valuable assistance rendered to
the conductors of the procession by the chief Con-
stable and the polio on the occasion. And that
the secretary forward a copy of this resolution to
his worship the Mayor."
Votes of thanks were also awarded to Mr. D.
Guile, London; Messrs. Austin and Shorrocks,
Manchester, and several others, for their attend,
auce and assistance at the meeting.

Some very strong remarks were made upon
the churchwardens for not allowing the bells
to be rung, and a great amount of sympathy
manifested towards the members of the
rifle band. Everyone present was of
opinion that the demonstration was a complete
success in every way, and as there is a balance of
between nine and ten pounds (being considerably
augmented by the kindness of the ehurchwarde a)
left from the subscriptions to the Demonstration
Fund, it was decided to send the surplus to assist
the Warwickshire agricultural labourers in their
present struggle.

SHEFFIELD.
CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.
The trades unionists and non-unionists o•

Sheffield, consisting of members of the societies or
unions of the Railway Spring Makers, File
Smiths, File Hardeners, File Grinders, Edge Tool
and Wool Shear Grinders, Seissor Forgers and
Scissor Grinders, Scissor Trade (workboard hands),
Rollers and Roll Turners, Printers, Shear Forgers,
Steel Melters, Fork Makers, Spring Knife Cutters,
Coopers, Joiners, Stone Masons, Smiths and
Hamrnermen, Thick Wire Drawers, Coach Buil-
ders, Labourers, Trippot-lane and Attereliffe
branches, Painters, Slaters, Cordwainers, Sweeps,
Fork and Spoon Filers, Plumbers, Bricklayers,
Silversmiths' Tinners, Razor Grinders, Comb
Makers, Blade Forgers, Table Knife Halters,
Associated Engineers, Ironfounders, Sickle
Forgers, Saw Grinders, Stove Grate Grinders,
-Typographical, Amalgamated Engineers, Hatters,
Coach. Trimmers, Brass Turners, Hammer
Drivers, Puddlers, Brace 13it Forgers, Brace Bit
Grinders, Patent Scythe Grinders, Boiler Makers,
Fender Makers, Patent Scythe Forgers, Pen and
Pocket, Knife Grinders, Cork Cutters, Basket
Makers, Button Makers, Glass Cutters, Awl Blade

Makers, Wood Turners, Brick Makers, Black-
smiths, Shot Makers, White Metal Smiths, and
other kindred societies, have presented a petition,
through Mr. Mundella, backed by nearly 6,000
signatures, against the Criminal Law Amendment
Act, 1871 (Violence, Threats, &c.). The peti-
tionerd regard the Act as an encroachment upon
their liberty of action as workmen, and respect-
fully submit that no just grounds exist for the
working classes being made the subject of excep-
tional legislation. They submit that the Act is
likely to be made the means of oppressing the
rights of labour in its contests with eapital, and
the slightest acts are liable to be construed as
coming within one or more of the clauses of the
said Act, Old such clauses can be niade use of by
employers to the disadvantage of their workmen,
some of whom may unwittingly fall in its clutches.
The petitioners also submit that the words
"molest or obstruct," as in the said Act defined,
are of so sweeping a tendency that on the
slightest disputes occurring between masters and
men the acts of the latter cannot fail to be con-
strued as coming within one or more of the Acts
which are defined to be by the said Act molesta-
tion and obstruction. Also, that there is nothing
in the Act to mitigate its severity, and that its
provisions are so vogue that no workman,
unionist or non-unionist, is safe from imprison.
ment while the Act remains in force.

articles.text:
NORTHAIIPTON.

THE WAGES QUESTION IN THE SHOE TRADE.

At Northampton, on Wednesday, a meeting of
the shoo manufacturers was held to take into con-
sideration the demand made by the stitched men
for ax increase of wages, and after a long discus-
sion the manufacturers decided not to recognise
the trade union, but expressed their willingness to
consider the matter individually, and, if necessary,
make an increase accordingly.

articles.text:
BATLEY.

BREACHES OP TUB MASTER AND SERVANTS ACT.

At the Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Abraham
Newsome, a foreman rag grinder, was summoned
by Messrs. Ephraim Fox and Sons, Steffe, for
leaving their service without proper notioe. Mr.
Ibberson, Dewsbury, appeared for the complain-
ants, and Mr. C. R. Scholes, j an. (Soholes, Dreamy,
and &holes), for the defendant. Mr. Joe Fox, a
partner in the firm, proved that notices were
posted in the mill requiring their workpeople to,
give a fortnight's notice before leaving. The
defendant gave a week's notice on the Monday
before Easter, and left on the Thursday following
and they claimed a fortnight's wages, a 12s. as
compensation. The defence was that the defen-
dant was engaged before the notices were posted,
and that he gave a week's notice, which he con-
sidered sufficient. As Good Friday happened in
that week the works stopped on the Thursday
night, and he was justified in leaving them.
The magistrates ordered the defendant to pay
1 Ss., the amount of one week's wages and
costs.

Benjamin Senior Ackroyd appeared to a sum-
mons charging hira with having left the service of
Messrs. Thos. and J. B. Jubb, manufacturers,
with whom he was apprenticed to learn the trade
of a cloth dresser. The indenture showed that he
was apprenticed for six years in October, 1866,
and it was stated that he left the service of the
prosecutors on the 15th April, or five months
before his term of apprenticeship had expired.
It was contended by Mr. C. B. Soholes, jun., for
the defence, that the complainants agreed to find
a man to teach him the business, and that they
had not done so for three and a half years, and
that therefore there was a breach of covenant on
their part. Witnesses were called to prove this,
and that the defendant did not understand his
business. The Bench were of opinion that the
defendant was bound to fulfil his contract, and
ordered him to find sureties in the sum of £2O
for his returning to complete his term of appren-
ticeship.

MISCELLANEOUS TRADE NEWS

ALTIIINCHAM.—The strike of painters at Altrin-
cham and Bowdon has come to an end, the masters
having acceded to the demands of the men for an
advance of wages from 61d. to 7d. per hour, and a
reduction of the hours of Tabour from 68 to 54i per
week.

BLACKBURN.-0 wing to the restrictions placed
upon the employment of children in brick- fields by
an act of last sassier, " carriers-off " have become
scarce at Blackburn, and the result has been a
demand by them of an increase of 2d. per 1,000
bricks. The brickmakers have asked the masters
for the extra 2d.; and the latter having refused
to pay it, the men have struck work.

LtteHsren,—The bakers' strike has terminated
by the ooncessT.on of an advance varying from three
to six shillings per week.

DUAIFRIES.—The masons are on strike, in con-
sequence of the employinent of slaters in pointing
the fronts of houses.

MANCHESTER.—The memorial from the builders'
clerks of Manchester and the district to their
masters, asking for a reduction of working hours,
was presented on Monday. The masters expressed
a willingness to grant concessions, but stipulated
that each firm should be free to make its own
arrangements, according to the exigencies of
business. •

NormanAm.—After a strike of seven week
the saddlers and harness makers, who demanded
an advance of 10 per cent. in wages and a reduction
of one hour per week, by leaving work at four
o'clock on Saturday instead of five, have obtained
a concession of their full demand from six of the em-
ployers. Four of the masters still hold out, and the
strike, so far as their establishments are concerned,
will still continue. Upwards of 180 male and female
workers in the employ of Messrs. Lee and Gee,
hosiers, Roden-street, have come out on strike,
protesting against the system of fining and lock-
ing-out, "as opposed to English princi,ples of
liberty."
LBEns.—The strike of felting operatives I;ns re-
sulted in the formation of the Amalgamated Felt-

jug Operatives' Society. The strike of puddlers
Nfessrs. Whitham's Peeseveranee Forge, Kirk-

firm having conceded the advance of is. 6d. per
Cm asked for by the men, who will now resume
work as fast as the furnaces can be got ready for
them. _

MIDDLETOIC—A large meeting of the silk
weavers of Middleton and neighbourhood was
held on Saturday evening, to take preliminary
steps for the formation of a co-operative silk
manufacturing company, in consequence of the
masters refusing to concede an amended list of
prices. The project received unanimous approval.
LYDNBY.—The tin-plate hands in the employ
of Messrs. Alloway and Co., Lydney, Gloucester-
shire, were on Saturday conceded a 10 per cent.
advance.

Dno it BDA.—At a meeting of the Associated
Trades on Saturday, it was determined to assist
the labourers now on strike to hold out until their
demands are complied with.
SOUTIIAMPTON.—The sailors belonging to the

Peninsular and Oriental Royal Mail Steam, and
other shipping companies connected with South-
ampton, are agitating for an increase of wages.
Youranms.—The mania against working the
two-furrow ploughs appears to be spreading. On
Saturday one Wold farmer summoned two ser-
vants (out of six who struck), under the Master
and Servants Act, and claimed £3 compensation
in each case. There was no Bench, and fresh
summonses will have to he issued.
BIRMINGIIA7C—A novel strike has just taken
place in Birmingham. The labourers engaged in
the construction of the postal telegraphs in the
district received a short time ago an order forbid-
ding them to make overtime. Hitherto the men
have received 20s. per week, and have workad
overtime. In consequence of this privilege, as
they considered it, being withdrawn, they asked
that their wages should be raised to 245. per week,
urging the fact that they had to go away from
home to work. This request was not complied
with, and on Monday morning they went to the
head office in Birmingham and demanded the day's
wages, which was always kept in hand. The
money was paid them anti they left, and arc now
on strike. At a meeting of the operative
bakers and confectioners on Wednesday evening,
it was resolved to come out OR strike if the masters
do not forthwith grant a reduction of working
hours and an increase of wages.
LEAMINGTON.—At Leamington, the gardeners,
butlers, stablemen, and domestic servants have
commenced an agitation for a union "to secure
and protect them in their rights." On Monday
evening upwards of forty representatives of these
classes held a meeting in the •Temperance Hall,
and decided that a union was desirable; but the
number of branches of labour to be included gave
rise to a diversity of opinion, and the matter
stands over for future consideration. A provisional
committee was appointed to convene a general
meeting next week. Shorter hours and better pay
are the objects of the movement.

BOLTON.—Tho operative bakers have applied
for an advance of 2s. per week to their wages and
the abolition of night work. They suggest that
they should commence work at five o'clock in the
morning, except on Saturdays, when the time
should be three o'clock. The scale of wages
submitted is as follows : —First hands, 30s. ; second
hands, 265. ; third hands, 21s. per week; 60
hours to be termed a week's work, and overtime
to be paid for at the rate of Bd, the hour for first
bands and W. per hour for second and third hands.
AOCRINGTON.—Throe out of four of the master

bakers have granted their men the nine bon"
system. The men of the remaining employer
struck work on Saturday.
DIIIIII2OI.—Mr. George Graion, builder, of
North-road, has reduced the hours of labour for

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.

SurFoLx.—Several of the farm labourers at
Newton, near Sudbury, Suffolk, were summoned
before the magistrates at Bexford last week, op
the charge of "unlawfully hindering and inclest-
ing other labourers with a view to c nue
them to leave their work." Tho informtions were laid under 31 and 35 Viet., chap.
32, entitled "An Act to amend the criminal
law relating to violence, threats, aud intimi-
dation," passed last year. The master alleged
that in one of the cases he saw the men at work
in the fields ploughing before breakfast, and shortly
afterwards he saw them riding their horses home,
accompanied by a crowd of about fifty persons.
One of the defendants was riding one of the horses.
The complainant himself was not called. In the
second case it appeared from the evidence of the
same witness that the complainant had three -men
in his employ hoeing wheat, when three of the
defendants wont to them, and, although he warned
' them of the consequences, they all went off together,
and joined the labourers who had struck. One of
the complainants was called, and described what
took place, but said that the defendants merely
beckoned-to him and his mates when they were at
work, and told them of the strike. The men said
they were all agreeable, and would strike too; and
told their master they must join the company.
They then went away, carrying their tools with
them. The witness was much pressed, but reiterated
that he was quite agreeable to leave his work when
asked; he was in no bodily fear of the defendants,
and his tools had not been interfered with by them,
or he hindered in the use of them. Mr. Jones, for
the prosecution, submitted that there was a
"watching and besetting " under the Act. Mr.
Mumford, for the defendants, denied that the Ant
had any reference to the case at all, but was
passed to prevent the outrages of trade unionists,
and protect both master and man. It would be a
monstrous stretch of the law if any conviction in
the present instance took place, as there was not
the shadow of a case. The magistrates, after a
lengthened consultation, dismissed the cases on the
ground that no coercion had been proved. Mr.
Jones intimated that other evidence was procur-
able, and that probably there would be an appeal.
A large number of farmers were present during
the proceedings. Nearly all the men have resumed

advance of a shilling a week. The wages have

articles.title: LONDON CABDRIVERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON CABDRIVERS.

On 'Nosily night a laftp meeting of cabdrivers
was held at Cambridge-hall, Newman-street,
Oxford-street, under the presidency of Mr.
Roger Eykyn, M.P., for the purpose of consider-
ing the necessity of obtaining an amendment in
the existing Metropolitan Carriage Act. •
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said
he had attended that evening solely for the pur-
pose of hearing fitful the cabdrivers a statement of
the grievances under which they considered them-
selves to be labouring, in order that f he found those
grievances substantiated, ho should be able to
render them assistance in Parliament, or in other
ways.
The lion. Secretary (G. Stormont Murphy,
Esq.) then read a memorial which it was pro-
posed should be laid before the Home Secre-
tary by a deputation suggesting various
alterations in the existing law. The prin-
cipal suggestions were that the existing laws
relating to cabs should be consolidated into one
Act; thlt the privilege cab system should be
abolished, and-that the railway stations should be
open to the trade at large; that a hansom cab
be entitled to carry three passengers, and a four-
wheeler six passengers; that cab proprietors be
allowed to remove their plates on to any cab that
has been certified; that drivers should only be
required to give a ticket to a faro when demanded;
that a registration system, instead of a licensing
System, be applied to driven; that agreements
between a cabdriver and a passenger be made
binding on both parties, the passenger as well as
the driver; and that no cabdriver should be com-
pelled to take a fare when off the stand between
the hours of 12 o'clock at night and 8 o'clock in
the morning.
Mr. Sellers then moved—" That in the opinion
of this meeting it is advisable to consolidate the

existing cab laws into one Act as simple and easy
of interpretation as possible." In supporting
this proposition, the speaker referred ,to the
memorial in its different Clauses, and espe-
cially alluded to the restriction of the number
that a cab was allowed to carry. There were
occasions perhaps when the number should be
limited, in the ease for instance of Irish funerals,
but be thought that a hansom should he allowed to
carry three persons if the " fares'' wished it, and
a four-wheeler six. It was often, too, desired
that a child should accompany the passengers, in
which he could see no harm. The speaker also
referred to the plate number, and thought that the
number might be transferred from one cab to
another, as it bore especially hard upon a " one-
numbered" man that he had not this privilege.
The system of giving tickets was also ridiculed by
the speaker in a humorous way, who asserted that
often when a cabman was desirous to give a ticket
(which were often kept under the seat in the cab
to keep them dry) they were urged by the" fare"
to drive on and never mind the tieket. He certainly
thought that the giving of tickets should be left until
they were asked for, and then, only on the refusal
of the cabman to giv e one, should he be held respon-
sible for any illegality. In conclusion, he said
there was a class of riders whom they all knew,
ho expected—namely, the non-paying riders, those
rascals who ride about in cabs, and then refuse,
on some trifling cause, to pay their fare. He
thought they should be made to leave at the
station-house something more than their name
and address, which in a great many eases were both
incorrect.

Mr. Conolly seconded the proposition, and said
there was one subject that had not been mentioned
by the last speaker, and that was the proposition
to abolish the present system of licensing and the
wearing of the badge, and to let the number of
the cab be a sufficient guarantee for the public.
He believed it would be a greater advantage than
at present, and would prevent much unnecessary
interference of the police; it would ensure a better
class of drivers—a better understanding between
master and man—in fact, a better state of things
altogether; and would eventually bo for the benefit
of all—the public included. In various instances
he showed the fallacy of the present system, notably
in the number of things that had been left at the
Lost Property Office, but' which were not claimed
by the public. The badge did not correspond
either with the number of the cab or the number
of the ticket, and hence the confusion and mis-
takes. The number of the cab would be a suffi-
cient protection for the public and the proprietor,
who was alone responsible for the action of the
driver if the latter could not be found. Mr.
Conolly then alluded to the iniquities of "The Red
Book," which he explained (at the request of the
Chairman) was a book in which the name of every
man who had not paid up his full money, or in any
way disagreed with his master, was entered, and
the speaker said it was impossible for that man to
obtain employment at any other yard while his
name was in that. book. In further reference to
the badge, he said it was high time it should be
abolished, as it was no good to the drivers, to the
public, to the proprietor, or to the police, for the
latter were often afraid to go on with a case fur
fear of making a mistake in the number, and by so
doing not obtaining a conviction. (Cheers.)
Mr. Norton, in supporting the proposition,
spoke against the present system of licensing, and
was sure that any alteration would be of benefit
both to proprietor and driver. He spoke
against the system of the Rod Book, and also on
the question of special arrangements that were
often made by passengers, and which, although
made by the latter, could not be considered bind-
ing, there being no redress for the cabman if they
refused, on arriving at their destination, to pay
him a promised 6(1. or Is. extra for driving fast to
catch a train, or for getting out early in the morn-
ing to take a special fare ordered the previous night.
If" cabby" reminded the of their promise he
was very often bullied, and asked if he had not
his right fare. He urged that agreements
such as these should be binding on both
sides. He also wished to see old and
infirm cabdrivers placed as attendants ors the
different ranks (cheers), so that the driver, when
his cab was unbircil, might have an opportunity
of getting his meals like any other man. At
the present time this was an impossibility, and if
his suggestion were adopte,l, it woald prevent
many front being summoned. He wished, in
conclusion, to draw the attention of thf,
meeting to the many advanta;es of the Cab
Drivers' Benevolent Association, which had been
the means of getting up this meeting. lie ex-
plained its benefits ; foremost among which was
the legal assistance it rendered to its members ;
out of about 300 summonses that had been taker
up by their solic:tor, he believed he could any that

GO out of every 100 had been got off (cheers), and
there were less summonses now on that account
than before the society was established. He
called attention to the fact that their noble chair-
man had promised to give them the ground whereon
to build their almshouses (loud cheers), and this
should induce those who had not already joined to
do so at once. They had a large number of the
nobility and gentry on their list of patrons (which
Mr. Norton read), and he begged to call special
attention to their noble treasurer (the Marquis of
Townshend) and their excellent chairman on this
occasion, and also to their kind and worthy hon.
secretary, all of whom were always working most
heartily and earnestly on their behalf. (Loud
cheering.)
The Chairman said that as there were evidently
storms and breakers a-head in the politiealhoriz on,
he was anxious to be at another place. He wished,
however, to state that the cabmen of London had
his entire sympathy. In their hon. secretary they
had a most restless man, for he was continually
inducing many gentlemen to take up the cause of
the cabmen. He was pleased at seeing the very
orderly eonduct of the meeting, which must go far
in their favour in the minds of ordinary observers.
Out of about seventeen Acts of Parliament which
were in existence at one time in reference to
public vehicles, they had nearly all been consoli-
dated, but this, not sufficiently to render the laws
perfect. The remarks of the speakers he had heard
were very forcible, and it would be their duty to see
bow they could amend the laws. For himself,
they could command his hearty support. (Cheers.)
The London cabmen, in his mind, were labouring
under a false stigma. Ile had been told by the
Home Secretary that there had been more parcels
given up as being found in public vehicles in the
past year than ever before, and this was a good
sign. Believing that they had fair and reasonable
ground for complaint, he would suggest that their
ideas on this subject be embodied in a memorial,
and when ready for presentation, he would under-
take to present a deputation. He must defend the
Government in teis mach, that it was never the
intention of the State to impose a hardship :on any
class. If he should be in Parliament, however,
next Session, he would undertake, in the absence
of the Government doing so, to introduce a Bill
for the better regulation of public vehicles. He
thoroughly endorsed the views of Mr. Norton in
reference to the Cabdrivers' Benevolent Associa-
tion, and advised the men to read a book called
"Self-help," and he should be happy to present a
dozen copies of the work to be lent out to the
members of the Society. (Cheers.)
Captain Maturin proposed, in a most felicitous
speech, a• Tote of thanks to the chairman,
and dwelt upon the advantages of the
Benevolent Association. He said they were obliged
to the members of the press for bringing their
objects before the public, and he hoped if any of
the philanthropic part of the community hal any
of those bank-notes that they occasionally sent to
other benevolent societies to spare, they would
not forget their hard-worked and deserving
servants, the London cabmen. (Loud cheers.)
A member in the body of the halLasked if this
meeting really intended to abolish the grievances
caused by the Red Book, and cited a case of great
hardship in proof of the desirability thereof.
The chairman, in reply, said the more immediate
objecc. of the meeting was to got an alteration in
the law. The Red Book, as ho took it, was a
sort of trades union among the masters, and no
doubt would eventually be done away with.

(Cheers.) He thanked them for receiving his
name as their chairman in such a hearty manner,
and again assured them of his support and in.
threat. Mr. Eykyn then left, and the chair was
for the rest of the evening occupied by Captain
Maturin.

Mr. Sawyer then proposed, in a most forcible
and practical speech, "That this meeting is of
opinion that the privilege system should be
abolished, and that for the convenience of travel-
lers the railway stations should be thrown open to
the trade at large." He gave instances where it
would be an advantage alike to the trade and to
the public if this monopoly were stopped. The
motion, being seconded, was carried unanimously.
A deputation of the principal members of the
trade was then appointed to form a memorial for
presentation to the lionie Secretary.
A vote of thanks to the chairman (Captain
?iliturin), the other friends of the society, and to
Vie hon. secretary, closed the proceedings.

MEETING AT TWICKENHAM.

On Sunday last a large meeting was held at
Twickenham, at which Dr. Baxter Langley de-

was frequently interrupted by applause. C. Whitby,
Esq., banker, took the chair, and expressed his

conclusion passed an enthusiastic resolution to join
the Amalgamated Society. Votes of thanks to
Dr. Baxter Langley and the chairman were carried
with acclamation. The room was densely .crowded.

SATURDAY, APRIL 27, 1872.

THE WEEK'S ALARM.

THE Education question'threatens to be the
death of the GLADSTONE administration. But
if so, the case will be one of suicide. Mr.
Etwcur's Bill for the Reform of Trinity
College, Dublin, is the apparent occasion. It
is divisible into two parts—one repealing all
tests as between different denominations of
.religionists; the other reconstructing the
College (or University, as it is in fact) upon a
new basis. To the repeal of the tests Minis-
ters make no objection; but they have their
own views on the remainder of the subject-
matter ; and on these views, it is understood,'
they will take their stand, and put it to the
House of Commons to pronounce, whether, as
a Government, they have, or have not, the
confidence of Parliament.

On Mr. FAwcErr's going into Committee
with his Bill, the Marquis of HARTINGTON,
therefore, is to make a motion which will have
the effect described.

That stage was to have been reached on
Tuesday. night. Instead of this, however,
Mr. FA.wcErr said, if the question had been
put to him on Friday last, he should have
persisted; but if there were any truth in
rumours industriously circulated, the measure
now occupied an entirely different position,
and different from what he ever supposed' it
would occupy; and therefore, if the motion of
the noble lord was to involve the question of
confidence in the Ministry he should consult
the House and also the Government as to the
time they would like the debate to coma on,
Mr. GLADSTONE, observing that no overture
had been made to him on the subject, said
that he could not give an answer without a
few days' notice; but before the rising of the
House, the Committee on the motion of Mr.
FAwcirrr was fixed for Thursday in this week.
The Bill, but for this party movement, was
expected to pass the Ciirrunons by a consider-
able majority; and, under the charge of Lord
CAnnts, with the approval of some Conserva-
tive Peers, was thought likely to get through
the House of Lords with but little opposition.
On Monday, however, the Daily News was
enabled to make known, that Lord HARTING-
TON'S amendment, accompanied by a pledge to
'resist the principle of denominational en-
dowment for educational purposes in
Ireland, would be moved as a test of confi-
dence in Ministers. This, of course, put
thoughtful Liberals upon mature consideration.
To reject Lora HARTINGTOWS amendment
would be to turn out a Government avowedly
Liberal. Useful legislation would be inter-
rupted, for the sake, at best, of taking up this
Session an Irish matter, which might as well,
and perhaps better, be disposed of next Ses-
sion. "Taking up," we say; for what would
be likely to become of such a measurt as the
Radical PROFESSOR'S in Tory hands? He saw
beforehand the real value of his new friends,
who, on Tuesday night, instead of enabling
him to bring on the Bill, helped to talk on
other subjects until it was too late. It is a
measure which ought to owe its success to the
honest sympathy of right-minded men. The
principles involved in it are far too high and
sacred to be made subservient to party tactics.
We shall rejoice, therefore, to see the Tory
intrigue utterly defeated; but we should
rejoice rather to hear Mr. GLA.DSTONE, as head
of the Ministry, and Leader of the Liberal
party, 'come out with the clear declaration of a
sound and sincere policy, wholly irrespective
of the votes of a small knot of members who

receive their inspiration, or perhaps their
orders, from quarters entitled to small consi-
deration in our Imperial Parliament.

Mr. FAWCETT asked the PRIME MINISTER,
on Wednesday, whether, as it had been stated
that the Government would consider the
decision of the House on Lord HARTINGTON'S
motion as involving a vote of confidence, he
would, according to usage, fix a day for its
consideration? Mr. GLADSTONE began
lh
conciliatory tones. If only Mr. FAWCETT'S
" recital " were correct, nothing would be more
reasonable than his request. But he at once
challenged its accuracy.. Here was a new sur-
prise in store for the unsophisticated listener.
Indeed, many listeners who could hardly be
thus described were, we venture to think,
deceived this time. It was perhaps expected
by some of those present that Mr. GLADSTONE '
was about to throw some doubt over, or
involve in some manner of qualification, the
statement which was mede early in the week.
He stated explicitly that the Government
had made up their minds to take the course
that had been described. Mr. GLADSTONE'S
words are: "A negative," he said, "put by the
Heusi?' to the motion of my noble friend the
SECRETARY for IRLAND, would, in our judg-
ment, fairly imply that the House was pre-
pared, if it thought proper, to entertain as a
settlement of the important questions con-
nected with the Dublin University the bill of
my honourable friend (Mr. FAWCETT) on its
present general basis, not only as to the Test
clauses, but as to the reconstruction clauses.
In our view, the adoption of that Bill would
place us in a condition which would
render it totally impossible for us to ask
the House to enable us to redeem the
pledges giveii to the country at the
end of the year MS. If we were
placed in such a position as to take out of
our hands the power of fulfilling those pledges,
we could not continue with credit to ourselves
and satisfaction to the House and the country
to: be responsible for the conduct of
_public
affairs." The Government, therefore, one
would suppose, accepts Mr. FAWCETT'S Bill as
involving a question of confidence. But Mr.
GLADSTONE drew a distinction between a
motion challenging the confidence of the
country in the Government and a measure like
Mr. FAWCETT'S, which, he said, only contained
a proposition the acceptance of which would,
as a probable, but not as a logically inevitable
consequence, compel the Government to resign.
It would be establishing a dangerous precedent
if any member were thus to obtain the privi-
lege of stopping public) business. Mr.
GLADSTONE therefore declined to assist Mr.
FAWCETT to such an extent. All he could
do would be to let him know when
public business would allow Government to
suggest a day for the discussion; but ho saw no
likelihood of an early day. Mr. FAWCETT rose
in a moment, in defiance of cries of "Order."
He declared the principle laid down fatal to the
rights of independent members, and then gave
notice, that, unless Government came to some
more distinct understanding with him, he
would next day call attention to the subject.
He will ask Government for some day before
the 15th of June ; and, if this be refused,
will bring forward a motion of censure.

A PROSPECT OF BETTER THINGS.
Tun land laid bare by the Metropolitan
improvements is to be made available to some
extent for dwellings suited to the working
classes. This is the nearly unanimous reso-
lution of the Board of Works. A clause in
the New Improvements Bill is to enable the

sale Or letting of sites along the lines of
alterations, on condition that such buildings
• be built on them. The plots have been
seleeted by the architect to the Board. These
sites are to be held over for three years, and,
if not by that time taken for the purpose, the
restriction is then to cease. Some people
may call this "philanthropic meddling ;" but
in what way could the men help themselves?
All society is interested in working men being
housed commodiously for themselves and for
their work. The letting of laud is full of
restrictions, most of which have much less to
plead in their favour than this has. We are
very much obliged to Sir SYDNEY WATERLOW
for carrying this point. It is high time

1.

that vacant land in the very heart of the
town were disposed of, and what manner
better than this ? As an investment
the thing will pay. The Industrial Dwelling's
Company, of which the worthy Alderman is
founder and chairman, has never paid less
than 5 per cent., and it has a demand for its
houses as fast as they can be built. Two
thousand houses more might be occupied next
week were they ready this. Let the Corpora-
tion of the City of London follow the example
of the Board of Works, and let Parliament
give sanction to them both"; and a pressing
want would be supplied to the general con-
venience in a manner hardly second to that
of the class who seem to be more immediately
interested.

articles.title: LIBERATION SOCIETY.
articles.text:
THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.

Jr will be seen from an advertisement in
another part of our paper, that this society is
to hold its annual meeting at the Metropolitan
Tabernacle next Wednesday evening, and we
are glad to see that it is to be presided over
by Mr. ISAAC HOLDEN, who lately fought so
good a battle for the society's principles in
Yorkshire, and who, we may add, is one of the
most influential laymen of that section of the
Wesleyan body who are supposed to sympathise
least with the objects of the society.
Probably, no speakers on the society's
platform have ever had such a choice of topics
of interest and importance, or have addressed
a meeting at a more critical period in the
history of the society's movement, than the
gentlemen who are to sustain the proceedings
of next Wednesday evening. Its interest will
be all the greater from the fact that it will be
held a few days before Mr. Mau, submits to
the House of Commons his motion for a com-
mission to enquire into the value and amount
of Church property. _ _

As the working classes have of late dis-
played increased interest in this question, we
hope that they will help to swell the numbers,
and to add to the enthusiasm which will, no
doubt, characterise the approaching meeting.

articles.title: RISING OF CARLISM IN SPAIN.
articles.text:
THE RISING OF CARLISM IN SPAIN.

THE Carlists of Spain .appear to think that
their time for making a supreme effort to gain
the throne is arrived. In some countries the
success of the present Government at the
polling booths would be a discouragement to
rebellion; but not so in the Iberian Peninsula.
The friends of the PRETENDER in the new
Cortes form a tenth part of the body. They
are resolved upon seceding; and they urge the
Republican section to follow their example.
Could these two elements be combined in an
organised resistance, it might be formidable;
but oil and water are not more unlike.
The question is, what King 'A:1111)MS
and his advisers think of doing ?
Should they accept the verdict of the
country, and proceed in the constitutional
path, well. The Carlists may be so headstrong
as to bring down destruction upon them-
selves; but it is to be hoped that the Re-
publicans will be better counselled than to
court a violent defeat, instead of continuing to
exert a moral pressure in a peaceful form. It
is to be hoped that the KING, who says he
knows his duty and will perform it, is inspired
with just views, and will understand the
infinite superiority of firmness with moderation
to intolerance with retribution. King AMADEUS
may well afford to receive with calmness the an-
nouncement which the PRETENDER makes from
the safe distance of Switzerland, that he is the
representative of religion and royalty for all
the world, and that, though he will regret to
shed blood, it will, soon be over, and himself
upon the throne. The Princes who, in or out
of France, seek :restoration in that conntry,
will net thank the " Duke of MADRID " for
making such an exhibition of himself.

THE AMERICAN QUESTION.
MINISTERS have again been questioned about
the negotiations respecting the Alabama Claims
simultaneously in both Houses. What the
questioners wanted to know was, whether
Government meant to go on with the Arbitra-
tion in the absence of any distinct assurance
of the indirect claims having been withdrawn.
At the present stage, neither Lord GRANVILLE
nor Mr. GLADSTONE thinks it proper to answer
, such an inquiry. The reply of the American

Government to our latest communication is on
the road, and will be here, perhaps, before the
appearance of •the present sheet, or, at any
rate, by Monday next. That reply may be
all that can be wished, or it may not. It is
best to wait and see which, and not in the
meantime to say what course would be taken
in a supposed contingency which may never
come to pass. This, however, did not satisfy
Mr. GATIIORNE HARDY, by whom, in the
absence of Mr. DISRAELI, the inquiry had been
put; and he forthwith announced that his
Right Honourable friend will embrais an early
opportunity of taking the opinion of the House
upon the subject.
In the meantime, it becomes more and more
evident that the indirect claims will be with-
drawn virtually if not
.expressly. The New
"Ircwl.: Times maintains that no publicist in the
States sanctions these claims ; and that, in
private life, it is rare to meet with any intelli-
gent man who defends them. "We are con-
fident of our position when we say," adds the
New York Times, "that, had they been
utterly omitted from the American argument,
not a voice would have been raised in
opposition. Indeed, we have strong reasons
for believing, that some of the United States
Commissioners themselves do not believe in
their admissibility or justice." Other papers
are in the same tone. The Washington Even-
ing Express says—" It:would be deplorable in
the interests of civilisation if the Treaty were
allowed to fail because one side asserts a false'
principle in law, in equity, and in reason, and
the other side refuses to meet ridiculous claims
by an argument of reason and fact." The
Evening Post says the United States will
sustain no loss of dignity if they recede. The
best American jurists condemn them. Con-
gress is almost unanimously opposed to thorn;
the mercantile community and the majority of
the press wish them withdrawn; only a mis-
taken pride and a false notion of dignity on
the part of the Administration sustain them.
A resolution has been passed by the House of
Representatives, calling upon the PRESIDENT to
furnish members with the official corre-
spondence respecting the indirect claims.

articles.title: FRENCH ARMY.
articles.text:
THE FRENCH ARMY.

THE nature of the lato rumours respecting
Germany and.,Franco gives interest to what
took place on the subject of the French army
on the resuming of business in the National
Assembly after the Easter recess. The
NIINIS'JCEU of the INTERIOR said that the new
taxes were very pressing. He was afraid,
however, that the report was not ready, and,
in that case, there was great urgency to
consider the Bill for the reorganisation of the
Council of State. M. GAMBETTA. exclaimed
that nothing could be more urgent than the
Bill on the Army. M. DAIHREL, the eminent
Rural, not ashamed on this occasion to agree
with M. GILAIDETTA, thought nothing more
important or pressing. The PRESIDENT of
the REPUBLIC, however, mounted the Tribune,
and, in fevi. words,
.said that the Bill on the
Council of State was very urgent. As to the
Army Bill, there were many points for dis-
cussion with the Committee—points better
discussed in private than in the Assembly.
His position made it essential, with reference
to the future of his country, that he should
personally take a leading part in the discus-
sion. His health made it necessary for him
to demand a respite, and he should not feel
equal to grapple with the question before the
lapse of three weeks.

REMAINING RELIGIOUS DISABILITIES,
Sin COLUAN CYLOGHLEN, On Wednesday,
moved the second reading of the Religious
Disabilities Removal Act. The main object is
to admit Roman Catholics and Jews to the
office of Lord Chancellor in England and
Lord-Lieutenant in Ireland. It also proposes
to repeal certain laws, never put into force,
against monastic institutions, and to remove
certain restrictions upon Roman Catholic be-
quests for religious purposes. Sir Comr.tx
gravely asked, why, if, in memory of old en-
counters, he were to leave a bequest for
masses to be said for Mr. NEWDEGITE, the
law should deprive him of such posthumous
advantage. After a long debate, Mr. BRVCIE
interposed while admitting that logically there
, was no reason for the oxolusion of Roman

Catholics from the office of Lord Chancellor
of England, he urged that public opinion
would not support the change, and recom-
mended the withdrawal of that clause. The
penal enactments, never enforced against
monastic orders, he totally condemned, and
declared himself anxious that some under-
standing should be come to with regard to
bequests for religious purposes. But a Bill
mixing up all these different subjects had
little chance of being carried. Sir' COLMAN
obtained time to think the matter over by
using his right of reply and talking the Bill
out.

THE FRENCH EX-AMBASSADOR ON
THE ENGLISH lIIINISTRY.

Tun Paris correspondent of the Daily News,
being in the same carriage with the Duke nu
BROGLIE between Paris and Versailles, heard
him openly make the following statement to
his fellow passengers :—ITe was interrogated
about what he thought of the situation of Eng-
land, and answered in a loud voice to his
deferential audience, "The English Ministry
is seriously shaken; the latest ehecl; is very
considerable." There could be no doubt of
the fall of the Ministry, were it not for the
extreme difficulty of replacing them. De
old Whigs, he said, were terribly frightened
at the prospect of an alliance between the
Tories and the Radicals. If Lord DERRY were
in the Commons instead of the Lords, his
opinion was that he, like CANNING, might
, succeed in forming a new party—the rdsult of
a sort of " fusion " between Conservatives and
the practical element of advanced ideas; but
he thought Mr. DISRAELI could not achieve
any such desideratum, and that, if he came
into power, a pure Tory Ministry was the
only thing to be expected.

articles.title: SCHOOL FEES QUESTION.
articles.text:
THE SCHOOL FEES QUESTION.

TIIE House of Commons will not now
reopen the discussion on the Elementary
Education Act. Mr. FORSTER, however,
admits that it will have to be reopened, and
that some day or other the 25th Clause will
have to be modified. Even Mr. BERESFORD
HOPE cannot deny it. Nothing but a great
pressure from behind could have forced 115
Liberal Members to vote for the introthition
of a Bill unconditionally repealing the Clause.
The minority, it will be seen, represents far
more actual experience of the working of the
Act, than the majority does. Mr. FORSTER
professes to think the irritation caused by the
power given to 13oards to subsidise denomina-
tional schools will soon disappear; but his
expectation is based on the hope that the
Boards will make as little use as possible of
their subsidising power. His argument is
Stockport. But there are places whorethe Town
Counoil and the School Board are at utter
variance. At the municipal elections in
November all will turn on denominational
subsidies. The delay is an encouragement to
both sides. Ott, the one hand it gives a pre-
mium to agitation, though, on the other, it
gives Boards an opportunity of showing
wisdom.

articles.title: EMIGRATION OF CHINESE COOLIES FROM MACAO.
articles.text:
THE EMIGRATION OF CHINESE
COOLIES FROM MACAO.

Further correspondence respecting the emigra-
tion of Chinese coolies from MAUI° has been laid
before Parliament in continuation of papers pre-
sented on the 14th of last July. The corre-
spondence refers to the rising of the coolies on
board the La Nouvelle Penelope, and the destruc-
tion by fire near Hong Kong of the Don Juan; which
had 650 coolies on board, 500 of whom perished.
Copies are given of the evidence taken in Hong
Kong from some of the survivors, showing the
system adopted at Macao for the collection and
embarkation of the coolies, and the manner
in which they are guarded during the
voyage. The Acting Governor of Hong Kong
says "that exertions aro used by the Portuguese
authorities to give to the emigration that freedoin
which can alone justify its maintenance there may
be good grounds for helieving ; but, on the other
hand, there is no reason whatever to doubt that
a large number of the coolies are deceived by
the countrymen through whose agency they are
collected, and that they are intimidated into giving
such answers to the inquiries made by the
authorities as are calculated to deceive them.
Moreover, there is the fact that they are imprisoned
during the voyage, and guarded so strictly as to
give every reasonable impression that there could

have been no desire willingly to emigrate for those
reasons which in such eases usually influence the
actions of men."

articles.title: BALANCE OF PARTIES.
articles.text:
THE BALANCE OF PARTIES.

The possibility of a vital division taking place
at no distant day has set both politieal parties
estimating their gains and losses since the general
election. When the present Parliament assem-
bled, on the 10th December, 1868, the number of
Liberals ranged under tbe leadership of Mr. Glad_
stone was 387, while the Conservatives mustered
only 271, thus giving the former a majority of
116. The first great division of the Parliament
took place on the morning of the 24th March, 1869,
when the second reading of the Irish Church Dis-
establishment Bill was carried by 368 to 250—a
majority of 118. Since that time the voting
power of the House has been diminished by six
members, Beverley, Bridgwater, Cashel, and Sligo
having been disfranchised. The losses were
equally divided between the two parties. During
the existence of the Parliament the Liberals have
won the following eight seats :—Bewdley, Bridg7
north, Dublin, London city, Nottingham, Norwich,
Stalybridge, and Taunton. On the other band,
the Conservatives have won eighteen seats—viz.,
Colebeitetr, Dumfriesshire, Durham, Glasgow and
Aberdeen Universities, Hereford, Isle of Wight,
Newry, Notts North, Plymouth, Shrewsbury, .
Southwark, Stafford, Surrey East, Surrey West,
Tamworth, Vitro, Wareham, and the Northern
Division of the West Riding. The balance of
advantage is, therefore, on the side of the Con-
servatives to the extent of ten seats, or twenty
votes. The Opposition now numbers about 290,
while the Ministerialists, including Whigs,
Radicals, Roman Catholics, Dissenters, and
Presbyterians are 360, a nominal majority of 70.

articles.title: FACTORY BILL.
articles.text:
FACTORY BILL.

Mr. Mundella has laid before the House of
Commons a Bill for further restricting the hours of
labour of children, young persons, and females in
certain factories. The Bill is to apply to factories
as defined in the Factory Act of 1844, as amended
by the Acts of 1846 and 1861, and to no other
factories, and the Bill is to be construed as one
with tho Factory Acts of 1850. and 1853. The
Intricacy of reference is rather troublesome. In
the factories to which this Bill applies, a child,
young person, or female is not, except in recover-
ing lost time, to be employed for more than 9/
hours on any day, nor for more than 64 hours in
any week, and not after 1 p.m. on Saturday, either
for recovery of lost time or for any other purpose.
The Bill also enacts that in certain sections (sees.
6 and 31 respectively) of the Factory Acts of 1850
and 1844 "0f hours" are to be substituted for
10/ hours; and certain sections (secs. 2 and 7 re-
spectively) of the Acts of 1834 and 1850 are to
be repealed. The Bill has on it the names of the
unusual, if not unprecedented, number of eight
members of the House, besides the member who
brought the Bill in; but there is no more limit in
that matter than in the number of bridesmaids.

M. Teisscrenc de Bort, the new Minister of

than in polities. As a railway director he has

stituent questions he is

Orl4anist ; fiscally he is an undoubted champion

material duties is thought to have been his
chief recommendation to M. Thiers.

articles.title: LONDON NATIONAL SOCIETY FOR WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.
articles.text:
LONDON NATIONAL SOCIETY FOR
WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

On Saturday, a meeting was held at the
Victoria Hall, Archers-street, Kensington, to
advocate the claims of women to the suffrage.
The attendance was large.
Mrs. Fawcett, Who presided, opened the
proceedings at some length. She said that they
would probably be accused of going over old
ground, but the question of female suffrage
must be gone over again and again until their
claim was adraitted. On the 2nd .of May Mr.
Jacob Bright's bill for removing the electoral
disabilities of women would be read a second
time, an they were not without hope that in
one respect at least Parliament might resemble
the unjust judge of the parable, who, when the
importunate came to him first, refused to hear
her appeal, but afterwards yielded, saying to
himself, "Though I fear not God nor regard
man, yet because this woman troubled me I
will avenge her, lest by her continual coming
she weary me." (Cheers.) They, gave fair
warning to those in the House of Commons
who opposed female suffrage, and though they
feared not justice nor regarded consistency,
yet they must know that there was a settled
intention on the part of women to weary them
continually until they granted their request.
(Loud cheers.) It was said that they had
altogether failed to prove that women them-
selves cared for the franchise, but meetings in
support of women's suffrage had been held all
over the country, which had been largely at-
tended by women of all classes, and who had
shown the greatest enthusiasm on the subject.
Referring to the injustice women suffered by
the present state of the Divorce Act, and from
what Mr. Gladstone had said in speaking on
Mr. ,Taeob Bright's Woman's Disability Bill of
last year, she thought they might draw the
conclusion that the right hon. gentleman
warmly sympathised with some of the wroi4s
of women, that it would not be long before he
had thought three times on the question; and
they might, therefore, hope he would soon be
reckoned amongst other distinguished sup-
porters of Mr. Jacob Bright'sßill. (Hear, Hear.)
If women suffered from unjust laws, they also
suffered even more from laws which were not
unjust, but which were unjustly administered.
Mrs. Fawcett then alluded to the difference in
sentences in criminal cases and contrasted the
seven years'. penal servitude and forty lashes
with the oat given to a robber who knocked a
man down and tried to steal his watch with
the three months' awarded a brute who pushed
his wife under a dray on London Bridge; and
the four menthe' to the ruffian for knocking
out the eye of his mistress. Lastly, there was
the case of the drunken ruffian at Preston,
who put his wife on the fire* and burnt her to
death, the coroner's jury returning a verdict
of manslaughter! If that wawanslaughter,
what was murder? (Loud Cheers.) There could
not be a case of a more brutal and disgusting
Murder. The chairwoman coneluded by saying
that what she had said proved that . their
grievances were not sentimental, but real.
(Cheers.)

articles.title: OLDHAM TRADES AND THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT.
articles.text:
THE OLDHAM TRADES AND THE
CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT
ACT.

THE following is Mr. GUILE'S speech at the
demonstration held at Oldham on the 13th :
Mr. A. Guile said it had already been intimated
by the chairman and other speakers that the Act
in question stamped a certain class of men as
trades unionists, and next branded them with a
mark, so that they stood distinct item all other
classes of men. As workmen, they said, that any law
like that under consideration operating as it did, on
one class of people only, was a bad law and ought to
be speedily repealed. (Hear, boar, and cheers.)
It was an unjust law, and deprived them of those
rights and privileges which theyougbt to enjoy in
common with their fellowman. (Hear, hear.)
Why was the exception made? Were there more
trades unionists in gaol than non-unionists? He
contended that there were not. They stood in an
elevated position. so far as crime was concerned,
and they were in a higher position in regard to
their independence. (Cheers.) Why was it so
Simply, because they managed to accumulate
funds, they put by their ponce for a future day,
when they themselves and their fellowmen re-
quired support through being overtaken by cit.
el:instances over which they had no control.
When they were old, and, could not work to sus-
tain themselves, proN i ion was made for them out
of the funds; they wore not found standing, bat
in hand at the workhouse doors, a craving for
parish relief. (Hear, hear.) They went t their
unions and applied to their brother-unionists, as
they had a right to do, for support to keep them
from starvation without troubling any o le.
(Cheers.) Then, for doing this, were they to be
branded as felons? They kept their wives and
children by the funds of their unions, from re-
ceiving parish relief, and took their members LA a
certain age, and said to them, "If we cannot keep
you as you were kept when you were young and
strong, and in the receipt of good wages, at least
we will do something towards helping you to live
out comfortably the remainder of your days."
(Cheers.) Their aged members were seldom
found in workhouses. (Hear, hoar.) If by any
accident a member became incapacitated from
following his employment, provision was made
for him. Then, he asked, wore those the doings of
criminals and wrong-doing men? Three societies,
belonging to the amalgamated engineers, had, in
the course of twenty-four years, paid no less a
sum than £1,500,000 in cases of death, sickness,
and old age. (Cheers.) After that the voice of
England would loudly deny that trades' unionists
should be branded as criminals. The wotkmen of
England were England's wealth, her independence,
her true nobility, and, being her true nobility, she
said, with one voice' that her workmen would
not submit quietly to be. branded as felons.
Oldham people said that day that they
would not be held down as felons by the
Criminal Law Amendment Act. (Cheers.)
They were the lever which worked the English
senate, and they were able either to keep it up or
cast it down. The speaker next proceeded to
give in detail the benefits arising to members
through the application of trade union funds, and
said that the workman had as much right to
defend his trade as the Church of England parson,
the lawyers and the doctors, had to defend their
professions. Workmen ought to be able to de-
fend their respective trades, and demand for their
labour the best price they could get. (Hear, hear.)
As an employer bold back his goods, to await a
favourable retain of prices, so ought a workman
to regulate his labour, so as to make it profitable.
It was their right to do so, and they ought to
battle for it, never resting satisfied until they
could feel as free as Clod intended they should be.
(Cheers.) .They had got freedom to a certain
extent. If the fetters which bound them wt n
not entirely broken, they were cracked, and, as
trades unionists, they would not rest satisfied until
they bad broken the last link in the chain, and
stood free men on England's free ground. (Loud
cheers.) He next advised his hearers to keep up
an agitation until the Act was repealed, and to be
determined to vote for no member of parliament
whatever might be his polities, who would not
pledge himself to support a bill for the repeal of
.the At. (Cheers).

The folbwing is the petition which was

—The petition of the factory workers and in-

With legitimate enterprise or freedom of ibdustry,

That, within the period referred to by your

First.—By the exceedingly rapid motion of

Second.—By the general recourse to cotton of a

Third.—By the employment in the - cotton

oak-nice for the females and young persons

Your petitioners bee to remind your honourable

articles.title: BEER AND BRIBERY.
articles.text:
BEER AND BRIBERY.

In a farewell address to the electors of
Tamworth, Sir Spencer Robinson says :
"We were not successful, but we were not
disgraced. I believe the freedom and inde-
p_endence of this borough are dear to you all,
ou have struggled for the success of these
prinoiples before now; you have suffered for
them; and through defeat, notwithstanding
suffering, you have, on mere than one occa-
sion, achieved triumphal victory. Electors
and working men, your cause is good; it
'commends itself to every man's heart. Let
freedom and independence be your watch-
words. Rally round the men, and round
those only, who will adopt them. You have
accepted me as your champion in the contest;
I am proud of the trust you have put in me.
I will never forget the confidence you have
reposed in me, My duty and my pleasure
alike will be to stand by my friends, and
bring this battle to a successful issue.
Broken promises and violated pledges are but
too common at elections. A gallon of beer is
still a more convincing argument than the
best profession of politieal faith, or than years
of useful and honourable toil in the servioo of
our common country. Elections are still
decided not on the merits of the principles
possessed by the candidates, but by the will
of those who hold in their hands the material
well-being of the conscientious voters, and
who not only have threatened to use that
power, but have used it relentlessly and
cruelly against those who are too weak to
defend themselves. Lamentable as it is to
see men's consciences smothered in drink, and
oppressed by the strong hand of power, We
should be just, and
stigmatise far more
severely the tempter and the tyrant than those
ivho yield to the one or are beaten down by
the other."

cursion to Baden-Baden. •

According to intelligence from Livadia, the
congenial climate has already had a most
beneficial effect upon the shattered 'health of
the Empress of Russia. The Emperor returned
to Odessa on the 17th.

On Monday morning a return was published
of certificates of naturalisation issued to aliens
by her Majesty's Secretary of State for the
Home Department, giving the names and
descriptions of such aliens, and stating the
coantrics to which they belong. Since 1868
only one alien—namely, Pandeli Rath, 8.A.,
born at Marseilles—obtained the right of
sitting in parliament and being of her Majesty's
Privy Council.

At Middleton, near Manchester, on Satur-
day, the funeral took place of Samuel Bam-
ford, one of the Peterloo riot leaders, and
author of" Celebrated Passages in the Life of
a Radical." A large procession followed the
hearse, and a meeting was subsequently held,
when it was decided to erect a public memorial
to his memory.

As the northern express passed Ditton
station, about half-past seven on Friday night,
the booking clerk at the station made an
attempt to cross the line, but he was caught
by the buffer of the engine, knocked down,
and the train went ..over him. When picked
up it was found tha his head had been com-
pletely severed from his body, and that one of
his feet had been cut off.

Lord Lichfield has signified his intention of
presiding at the inaugural banquet, to he held
on May 15, at the Foresters' new Hall in
Wilderness-row.

The splendid hall and offices recently erected
by the -London United District, at a cost of
some £lB,OOO, will, we are informed, be re-
quired for the purposes of the Mid-London
Railway.

The Ancient Order of Poresters according
to the Foresters' Monthly Journal, have in.
creased their numbers by 19,581 during the
past year, while the sum of £96,000 has been
added, to the reserve fund. of courts and
districts. Taking into account the juvenile
societies and the second degree (the Ancient
Order of Shepherds), the members now
number more than half a million, having funds
invested to the extent of £1,527,939, as a pro-
vision against sickness and death.

It is announced from Paris that, notwith-
standing the representations made to it, the
Prench Government has refused to commute
M. Henri Rochefort's sentence to transporta-
tion to a fortress.

At a meeting of Liberals held on Monday,
arrangements were made for a requisition to
Mr. Robert Jardine, M.P. for the Dumfries
burghs to contest Dumfriesshire at the next
election in the Liberal interest.

With regard to the statement .as to the
release of Madame Rachel, it seems that the
prisoner was under sentence of five years'
penal servitude, which expires in September,
1873. Her conduct at Woking having been
good, her release was granted at. the ordinary
time on the usual ticket-of-leave, by which
the holder is bound to report herself personally
once a month at the district police-station.
As ti rule, all the ticket-of-leave prisoners are
inspected at "the Southwark prison" on a
Wednesday, and released on the ensuing
Saturday, as was the case last week with
several, the only difference being that Madame
Rachel was permitted to,leave on Saturday
last without being "inspected," and to take
up her residence at Kentish-town.

A. fatal accident has occurred at Hounds
Hill Colliery, Prince's End, by which one man
lost his life and another had a very narrow
escape. -Iwo field carpenters, named John
Bate and George Sadler, were descending the
shaft for the purpase of making some repairs,
when the pit rope slipped off the " drum " and
they were thrown out of the " bowlc." Bate
fell to the bottom of the shaft, a distance of
200 yards, and was killed instantly. When
picked up his body was frightfully mutilated.
Sadler succeeded in laying 'hold of the wire
guard, and whilst hanging in this perilous
position the engineer lowered a rope and
hauled him out of the shaft.

On Friday evening a man named Holden,
while in Menders' Menagerie, which is now
being exhibited at Shrewsbury, foolishly tried
to shake hands with a large Bengal tiger. The
greeting was not reciprocated; the tiger showed
his claws and Holden felt them. He is now
under surgical treatment.

It appears; from the Japan Mail, that the
government is disposed to abandon the one
course of action which has laid it open to
severe animadversion by foreigners. It has
ordered the native Christians who were
banished last December to be restored to their
villages. We hope it will go further' and
make a similiar order with reference to the
many hundreds who have been similarly
treated. It may allow the free exercise of a
religion without inviting the proselytism which
it seems especially to dread.

Yr. Registrar Pepys has had before him the
bankruptcy of Mr. J. C. Angerstein, a. young
gentleman who had just come of age, with
debts 'exceeding £14,000. His passing was.
opposed on the ground that he had not fully
disclosed his estate, but after the bankrupt had
been examined at some length, the Registrar
overruled the objection, and allowed Mr. An-
gerstein to pass, on condition that he continued
to give all the information in his power to the
trustees.

Notice is given by the Lord Chamberlain in
the Gazette that the presentation at Court of
Lady Twiss had been cancelled.

The sittings of the. English Presbyterian
Church were brought to a close on Monday.
The next Synod will be held at Newcastle-on-
Tyne.

In accordance with a resolution passed at a
meeting of Professors of the Royal Academy of
Music, nearly twelve months ago, a testi-
monial has been presented to Sir W. Sterndale
Bennett, as marking the cordial sympathy of
musical artistes in the honour which her Ma-
jesty had been pleased to confer upon him. The
gathering took place at St. James's-hall, the
Attorney-General in the chair.

Lord Penzance, on Tuesday, pronounced in
favour of the will of the late Miss Cordelia
Angelica Reed, the owner of the ruinous pro-
perty which for so many years disfigured the
south-vest corner of Stamford-street. The
old lady left the bulk of her fortune, amount-
ing to about £lOO,OOO, to the Hospital for Con-
sumption at Brompton.

A Berlin Correspondent says that the open-
ing of the new German Univerity at Stras-
burg on the Ist of May is to be a kind of
national festival. Invitations have been
addressed to the professors and students of all
the great German Universities to send depu-
tation, s to take part in the ceremony. The
opening Address is to be followed by a public
dinner, and in the evening there will be an
illumination of the spire of the Cathedral.
Festivities will also take place on the follow-
ing day. It is not apprehended that there
will be any altercations with the inhabitants,
as German rule has become rather popular
than otherwise with the lower classes, and the
higher classes, who are still French in feeling,
keep. in retirement. It is thought that a large
number of -German students will enter the
University. of Strasburg for the express pur-
pose of cultivating friendship with the young
Alsatians,

Mr. Hughes Mason, Chairman of the Man-
chester Chamber of Commerce, spoke ominously,
on the subject of Mr. Mundella's bill for re-
stricting the hours of work in factories. Raw
material was, he said, 70 per cent. higher than
last year, and the time was most unfortunate
for introducing legislative interference.

Dr. Thomas opened the spring session of the
Baptist Union of England and Wales, and
spoke at length on the education question. He
said that the Government were the worst of
educators, and he regarded Treasury grants for
education in the same light as State endow-
ments, to which Nonconformists had always
objected.

An eloquent appeal was made on behalf of
the Royal National Hospital for Consumption
at Ventnor by the Lord Bishop of Winchester,
who took the chair at the annual festival at
Willis's Rooms. Upwards of £2,000 was
collected during the evening; and one gentle-
man gave -11,500 in addition for building a
new block of houses.

At Gresham College, the Rev. 3.W. Burgon,
vicar of St. Mary's, Oxford, Gresham Lecturer
in Divinity, delivered. a lecture on the Atha-
no.sian Creed, in presence of a somewhat large
and most sympathetic audience. The lecturer
protested. against the rejection, mutilation, or
annotation of the creed.

At the Mansion-house on Tuesday, Mess rs •
Bryant and Jackson, lately in -business in
Wood-street, City, again appeared in answe r
to a summons charging them with having
obtained goods by false representations within
four months of their failure. The Lord Mayor
held that the allegations made on the part of
the prosecution had not been proved, and dis-
charged the defendants.

The Parliamentary Committee of the London
and. Provincial Licensed Victuallers have
published a series of obeetions to Sir
ltobert Austruther's bill relating to
the sale of intoxion,ting liquors, which&
stands for second reading on Tuesday
the 23rd inst. They affirm that the formation
of local districts and the election of licensing
boards is a direct recognition of the permissive
principle, and is in antagonism both to Sir S.
Ibbetson's Bill and that of the Government;
that the provision that no licence for music or
dancing shall be granted to any person hold-
ing a victualler's licence, or to any premises
adjoining a public-house, is unjust to the pre-
sent holders of music and dancing lieenees,
and introduces an entirely new principle of
licensing such places ; and that the clauses
respecting Sunday closing, the meetings of
benefit societies and clubs, and the prohibi-
tion of the employment of any person under 18
years for the supply of drink, are injurious,
oppressive, and unnecessary.

On Saturday last the Cunard Company's
steamer Scotia—now the only Atlantic-going
paddle steamer in the Cunard service—left
the Mersey for New York, with 160 saloon
passengers, amongst whom were the Countess
de. Dion, Lord and Lady Milton, and Mr.
Serjeant Sleigh and lady. We understand
that the learned serjeant goes out to America
on a mission in connection with the counter-
claims of a number of English merchants in

named Packer, between 50 and 601 years of
age, has committed suicide. The friends of the
deceased had left him in charge of the house,
and on their return at four o'clock the doors
were found to have been all secured. A forcible
entry having been effected, the deceased was
found hanging by his neck in the washhouse
He was immediately cut down, but life Was'

On Sunday a deputation, said to consist of
2,000 of the inhabitants of Rome, waited on
the rope. His Holiness, after stating that
the whole world admired the love the people of
Rome displayed towards him, severely re-
proached those by whom the rights of the
Church had been usurped.

There was animposing masonic demonstration
at Southampton on Tuesday, when the Mar-
quis of Ripon, Grand Master of England, and
most of the officers of the Grand Lodge, paid
a visit to that town. The proceedings in-
cluded the presentation of an address to Lord
Ripon by the Mayor and Corporation the
attendance of the masons in full regalia at
Divine service, and a concluding banquet.

It is stated in a telegram from Marseilles
that Prince Alphonso, the brother of Don
Carlos, has been requested to leave that town
and go to Switzerland, as he would not be
allowed to approach the Spanish frontier.
From Madrid news comes that the Culla
rising has "commenced," and that bands
commanded by a priest have appeared in
Toledo and Navarre. Considerable excite-
ment is said to prevail among the Carlists at
Pampeluna, Don Carlos being expected there
in person.

A meeting of the Metropolitan Board o
Works was hod the other day, at which a
report was read from the Parliamentary Com-
mittee recommending that power be taken for
providing house accommodation for the working
classes who will be dispossessed of their hold-
ings by the proposed improvements of the
Board. Three sites had been set aside for this
purpose. The report, after some discussion,

somewhere near A.kbarpore, in the district of
Fyzabad, a boy was found in the den of a
wolf, and has been brought to the dispensary.
The boy cannot speak, is very lean and emaci-
ated, likes to live in retired places, and de-
vours raw meat.

Over thirty thousand rupees have been sub-
scribed to the Mayo Memorial Fund in Cal-
cutta, A special memorial is proposed among
Indian sportsmen, the probable application of
which would be a scheme for improving the
breed of horses throughout the Peninsula.
To this, as a military question, Lord Mayo de-
voted great and successful attention during his
administration.

From Bombay we have intelligence of the
wreck of the ship Maria, belonging to the
Guinea expedition, with a loss of thirty-five
lives.

A disputed point in the history of the in-
fallibility dogma has been elucidated by the
Archbishop of Paris in his recent pastoral.
He affirms, in contradiction of what was not
a very rare opinion about a year ago, that the
dogma was subscribed by his lamented pre-
decessor, Monsignor Darboy. The latter
wrote to the Pope on the 2nd March, 1871,
expressing his adhesion, pure and simple, to
the dogma. The Pop 3 answered him in a
letter of March 20, which the late Archbishop
was never allowed even to read. While in
captivity he was so utterly isolated from his
flock that he had to leave unfulfilled his in-
tention of promulgating the dogma. His
correspondence with the Holy Father has now
been published.

Both Houses of Convocation re-assembled.
on Tuesday. The propriety of retaining the
Athanasian Creed was the special subject of
discussion in the Lower House.

The Convocation of the University of Oxford
have unanimously resolved to memorialise Mr.
Cardwell against that town being made a
military centre.

Duceleuoh, was hold in Edinburgh. on Tuesday,
at which resolutions were carried setting forth
the importance of religious instruction in or-
dinary schools and characterising as objection-
able several aatures of the Scotch Education
Bill now before Parliament.

the Council of the Charity Organisation So-
ciety, the members of which submitted pro.
posals for extending the usefulness of the

respect to the memory of the late vicar (Arch-
deacon Downall), and in order that the congre-
gations might attend the parish church, where

From an account which has been drawn up
at Berne we learn that the total expense in-
curred by the SwiSs Government in maintain-
ing General Bourbald's army during the late
war amounted to upwards of twelve million
francs.

Advioes from Rio de Janeiro state that the
Emperor and Empress of Brazil returned
there on the 31st March after their long tour
in Europe, and were enthusiastically received.

By the Cape Mail we learn that the news
from the diamond-fields is more desponding by
every post. According to the Cape Argus,
people on the spot, who are competent to judge,
think that a great reaction will take place iu

Her Majesty held a Drawing-room at
Bunkingham Palace on Tuesday afternoon,
and will hold another on May 6th..

Prince Arthur occupied the chair on Tues-
day night at the anniversary festival of the
City of London Hospital for Diseases of the
Chest. Subscriptions wore announced to the
amount of £4,700.

again mot on (.I:uesday, when evidenoe was

Last week the mortality in London and 20
other large towns of the Ignited Kingdom was
at the rate of 25 deaths annually to every
1,000 persons estimated to be living. In the
metropolis J,252 births and 1,410 deaths were
registered, the former having been 109, and
the latter 171 below the average. Forty-eight
persons died from small-pox, 77 from measles,
11 from scarlet fever, "7 from diphtheria, 72
from whooping-cough, 22 from different forms

16 as enteric or typhoid, and 3 as simple con-
tinued fever), and 13 from diarrhcea,. The
mean temperature was 46. , 2 and all but corre-
sponded with the average of the same week in
60 years.

A fire broke out a few days ago in a State
forest, near Pan. The prefect, having put in
requistion the services of a detachment of the
garrison, immediately proceeded to the spot;
but whilst they wore engaged in extinguishing
the fire on one side, the flames spread rapidly
on the other. Fortunately, the Lieut.-Colonel
of the 18th of the Line arrived with about a
hundred men, and their united efforts were
crowned with success. Abeut seventy-five
acres of young copse were consumed. The
disaster was attributed to the imprudence of a
smoker throwing away a still lighted cigar.

A death has recently taken place in the
army which, although it can scarcely be
chronicled in our obituary column, is never-
theless, not unworthy of note. " Tanby," the
celebrated antelope of the 7th Hussars, has
paid the last debt of nature. A post-mortem
examination revealed the fact that " Tanby "
had an ostrich-like capacity for eating singu-
larly indigestible substances. In his stomach
were found several brass knobs, a sponge, half
a yard of flannel, and sundry other articles
which are not generally recognised as articles
of food— even for antelopes. " Tanby's "
head and horns will, we understand, be pre-
served by the regiment in memoriam,

dition started, and its progress from I stage

Conservancy, it appears that four thousand
trout, of very large size, were turned into the

Glasgow being placed second, and Hector

Royal Geographical Society, letters were read
from Dr. Kirk, which, without giving anything
new respecting the fate of Dr. Livingstone,
expressed the conviction of the writer that the
intrepid traveller was still alive. Intelli-
gence has been received which threw some

pedition which had been fitted out to search

On Wednesday the Lords Justices and the
Master of tho Rolls were absent from their
respective Courts
,in Chancery, for the purpose
as declared by their lordships' court-papers, of
"sitting in the Privy Coupoil.' Their so-
journ in Downing-street, however, was not for
the purpose of hearing Indian and colonial
appeals, but, as it is known, to discuss anew
the
.judgment in "Shepherd v. Bennett,'
with regard to which their lordships have, it
is stated, arrived at an embarrassing dead-
lock. The Lord Chancellor some months ago,
in accordance with the opinion of the majority
of the Court, drew up a learned and elaborate
judgment favourable to the defendrust ; but
this document, it is understood, has not found
acceptance amongst a dissentient minoritynf
the Court, which is said to, include the two
clerical members, an ox-Chancellor of Ireland,
and. (upon a legal technicality) Lord justice
Mellish. • The question involved is one of
deep import to the future of the Church of
England, the charge against Mr. Bennett
being -one of heretical teaching upon the
subject of the presence of Christ in the Holy
Communion. The reverend defendant (by his
own choice) declined to plead before the
Court on conscientious grounds, and the case
was tried both in the Arches Court and on
appeal in his absence. It is possible that this
lack of assistance by counsel Co the Court may
have brought about the delay which has taken
place in arriving at a judgment; and, having
in view the abstruse nature of the question
involved, it is 'considered doubtful if a final
decision upon it be pronounced on this side of
the Whitsuntide Recess. •

journal o:lficial, appoints M. de Goulard

Windsor on Tuesday, previously to IN huh Mr.
Justice (Wain and Mr. Alderman Dakin, late
Lord Mayor of London, received the honour of
