made by the committee appointed by Govern-
Aunt to report on the suitability of that
building for a naval college. The inhabitants

mouth Pollee-court on Wednesday, it was

'The New York, Ilerald states that, in con-
sequence of the investigation ordered by
General Grant, it has been found that, during
the administration of Andrew Johnson, the
collection of the whisky and tobacco dues was
a mere farce. A " ring " was formed which
enabled its members to avoid the imposts levied
for the purpose of reducing the national debt,
and it is stated that its efforts were so success-
ful that the State has been defrauded of up-
wards of one hundred and sixty millions of
dollars. Prosecutions have been ordered against
a large number of people, and as many of them
are persons who lately occupied official posi-
tions and places of respectability and trust, the
discovery and its attendant litigation are
creating considerable excitement in all parts of
the States.

Intelligence received in Liverpool from New
York states that on the 9th inst. Deputy Sheriff
Judson Jarvis arrested "Lord" George Gordon,
alias George Henry Gordon, alias Gordon
Gordon, at the suit of Jay Gould, on an order
of arrest granted by Judge Brady. It appears
that Mr. Gould swears that on Ist March last
he delivered to Gordon 600 shares of Erie
'Railway stock, of the market value of 36,000
dollars, that he instructed Gordon to sell the
stook, and with the proceeds to purchase eighty
acres of land in Westchester county; and that
Gordon did not observe his instructions, but
refused to return the stock, and converted it to
his own use. Gordon, however, was released
from custody on finding bail in the sum of
37,000 dollars. But the most curious part of
the story remains to be told. Gordon is an
Englishman, who arrived in New York some
time ago, representing himself as a large Erie
stockholder, and claiming that he owned half
of all the stock held in England. He appeared
at the Erie office at the time of Gould 's over-
throw, and loudly demanded admission, which
was refused. He claims to be the Earl of
Aberdeen, whose fate was long in doubt, but
whose loss at sea appears ncw to he settled
beyond all dispute. Notwithstanding this,
Gordon is said positively to assert his identity
with the lost earl;and to declaroshis intention
of claiming the Aberdeen estates.

A. telegram from Madrid states that a
general Carlist rising is believed to be
imminent, and that great political agitation
prevails in the capital. According to another,
Carlist bands, consisting of armed peasants,
under, the command of the priests, have ap-
peared in several provinces. It is even
reported that one of the priests has been
captured and shot, his followers having pre-
viously been defeated. The number of bands
at present in the field is estimated by the
Correspondenoia at 30, the largest consisting
of not more than 300 men. It is stated, how-
ever, that the Carlist bands in Navarre
are composed of about 600 men. The Govern-
ment, it is believed, means to show no leniency
to the insurgents.

It is announced from Potsdam that the
Princess Imperial of Germany, the Princess
Royal of England, gave birth to a:daughter on
Monday evening. The Princess has now
seven children, viz., three sons and four
daughters.

Exchequer receipts amounted to £4,309,957, a

period of last year. The expenditure during
the three weeks was nearly seven millions.
The balance at the Bank exceeds five millions
and a quarter.

Revolution is again making way among the
Mexicans. It has extended to Yucatan which
is now in the powei• of the insurgents.

It has been decided by the Lord Justices, on
appeal from an interlocutory injunction
granted by Vice-Chancellor Bacon, that the
Great Eastern Railway Company have power
to close Sun-street, Bishopsgate, and to appro-
priate part of it for their new station.

William Turner has obtained from the
Court of Queen's Bench a rule nisi for the re-
covery of his daughter, a'girl about Ave years
of age, who remained in her mother's custody
after the marriage was dissolved by divoroe.
The mother was stated to be intemperate and
neglectful of the child. ,

Cuxhaven is said to have been selected by
the German Ministry of Marine as the site of
an Imperial naval station. With that view it
is to be strongly fortified, and its harbour
accommodation is to be developed to the
utmost.

Last week several large sailinf, vessels
bound from the Tyne for the East Indies and
the South, were detained through the inability
of the ship-masters to make up their orews.

Viotor Hugo's " L'Annes Terrible," is now
in the hands of the Parisian public. The
poet, in framing his calendar, has indulged
extensively in comparisons—personal as well
as national. The ex-Emperor and King
William are rival heroes of one of the most
vituperative strophes.

APRIL 27, 1872.

• A telegram from Geneva states that Don
Alphonso has arrived there from Marseilles, but
taht Don Carlos has disappeared since the 22nd
inst., and, is supposed to have left the town.
According to information received by th°
Epoca of Madrid, the Carlist bands are not on
the increase, and are being concentrated in
Navarre, where they are composed of 2,000
men. Despatches received by the Spanish
Goverment represent that the insurrection
already diminishing. Meanwhile Navarre,
Lerida, and Biscay have been declared in a
state of siege.

An official communication, which has bean
forwarded *from the Belgian Embassy in
London, states that the assent of the Belgian
Government to the extradition of Marguerite
Diblano was granted directly it was asked by
the French Government.

A. crowded meeting in connection with the
National Education League was held at Her
on Tuesday evening. Mr. Francis Adams,
the secretary, and the Rev. T. Horwood Patti-
son, honorary secretary of the Rochdale branch,.
represented the League. Members of all re-
ligious denominations were present, including
the Church and Roman Catholics. Mr. Touch-
stone represented the Union. A number' of
people were unable to obtain entrance. ReßO-
lutions in favour of the League programme
were carried by a majority of three to one.

Another child has died of small-pox among
the religious body at Plumstead known as
"The Peculiar People." It is believed thst
the custom of laying-on of hands, practised by
the elders of that body, has had much to do
in spreading the disease... The coroner said
they must be treated as mad persons, and care
taken that they did no more misohier. He
ordered that the elders should be present at
the next inquest, remarking that they would
probably find the law would reach them in a
way they did not expect.

At Marylebone Police -court on Wednesday,
Eliza Howard was charged with stealing a
diamond ring, the property of the Hon. Maria
Bingham. She had driven in a private
carriage to a pawnbroker's on several occasions,
and pledged various articles of jewollery.
The prisoner was remanded, being locked up
in default of finding the bail required.

A singular eve was before the notice of the
Clerkenwell police magistrate on Wednesday.
One M. Dupont, formerly residing in the
Tollington-road, Holloway, had been sum-
moned for having unlawfully detained a chest
of drawers. It was explained that the
defendant was not in attendance, for the sufa-
oient reason that he was under sentence of
death in Paris as a communist. The summons
was dismissed, and it was stated that, should
Dupont be executed, proceedings might pos-
*Ably be taken against his widow.

Two master lightermen, carrying 6n
business in Mincing-lane, were on Wednesday
committed for trial from the Idansion-bouse
on a charge of having fraudulently converted
to their own use property which had been
entrusted to them as bailees.

The Committee of the Ballot Society have
passed two resolutions, expressing satisfaction
at the course taken by the Government in
their conduct of the Secret Voting Bill, and
urging them to proceed with the measure in
spite of all opposition.

Amongst the speakers at the banquet of
the Institution of Civil Engineers, on Wed-
nesday night, were Prince Arthur, Mr. Glad-
stone, and Mr. Goschen. The other gather-
ings of the evening included the festival of the
United Grand Lodge of Freemasons and the
annual dinners of the Hospital for Incurables,
and the British Orphan

Sir Coleman O'Loghlon's Bill for the Aboli-
tion of certain Religious Disabilities was the
subject of a deputation to the Prime Minister
on Wednesday. It was introduced by Mr.
Aforley, M.P., and its members represented
the feeling of uneasiness which pervaded the
religious denominations at the growing de-
mands of the Roman Catholics. Mr. Glad-
stone reminded his hearers that the measure
had been introduced by a private member, and
that the Government were not responsible for
it. At the same time full consideration
should be given to the arguments and facts.
which had been laid before him.

In the Lower House of Convocation on
Wednesday the discussion upon the Athano.-
sian Creei was resumed by Bishop Parry,

number of petitions bearing upon the subject
of debate were presented.

articles.text:
IM.PERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDA.Y. •
THE BALLOT BILL.
Mr. W. Fowler intimated his intention to ,
introduce, on an early day, a Bill to repeal the
Contagious Diseases -Acts.
The Lord Advocate, replying to Mr. B.
Coehrance, promised to bring in the Scotch
Education Bill "as soon as the Ballot Bill
leaves this House. Mr. Cardwell promised to
consider what measures could be adopted to
preserve the graves of those who fell in the
Crimean war.
In reply to an inquiry from Lord Eleho,
the right hon. gentleman stated that it has
been decided that the autumn maneouvres for
the present year shall be conducted on Salis-
bury Plain, and shall commence on the 31st
of August; and that all parts of the United
Kingdom shall be represented in the forces
engaged.
Soon after the House went into Committee
upon the Ballot Bill, Mr. Bright took a seat
upon the Treasury Bench, and remained for
some time in earnest convdtsation with the
Prime Minister.
The fifth, sixth, and seventh clauses having
been agreed to, the first division was taken on
a proposal by Mr. Graves to permit sailors and
pilots compelled to go to sea between the day
of nomination and that of the poll to deposit
their ballot papers with the retuening officer
before their departure. The amendment was
supported by the representatives of many
maritime boroughs, but being opposed by Mr.
Forster, was rejected by a majority of 87-241
to 154.
After this decision the progress of the Bill
was steady and easy until the 12th clause was
reached. Mr. Ward Hunt moved the omission
of this section, which provides that no person
shall iu any legal proceeding to question an
election be required, or even without his con-
sent be asked, to state for whom he has voted;
but upon a division he was defeated by a
majority of 102-193 to 91.
Upon the 16th clause there was a prolonged
discussion as to the provision of polling places
in Scotland, but in the end the proposal of the
Government to maintain .things as they are in
that respect was carried by a majority of 05—
an amendment proposed by Mr. Gordon being
rejected by 155 to 90.
An amendment moved by Mr. 13ruen on the.
18th clause, with reference to the multipli
cation of polling-places in Ireland, was rejected
'by 83-219 to 136, and while the section was
still under discussion progress was reported.
The House adjourned, shortly after 2 o'clock.

HOUSE OF LOBDS.—TUESDAY.
The House was chiefly occupied with the
advancement a stage of a few Bills and the
ordering of some returns. .
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.
After the disposal of the questions, Mr. New-
degate moved ar leave to introduce his Bill
for a commission to inquire into monastic and
conventual institutions, and leave was given
after some discussion. Mr. Candlish then
moved for leave to bring in a Bill to repeal
the 25th clause of the Education Act, but on a
division the motion was uegatived by a ma-
jority of 201-316 to 115. A short time was
spent in the discussion of the propriety of
issuing a Royal Commission to inquire into the
Endowed Schools and 'Hospital of Scotland;
but in the end the debate was adjourned, and
after Mr. Fawcett had postponea the Univer-
sity (Tests) Dublin Bill till Thursday, and
some other business had been disposed of, the
House rose.

HOUSE 01? COMMONS.—WEDNESDir.
Almost as soon as the private business had
been disposed of, Mr. Fawcett asked the Prime
Minister whether, as it had been stated that
the Government would consider the decision of
the House on the instruction to the Committee
on the Dublin University Tests Bill, of which
the Marquis of Hartington had given notice, as
involving a evote of confidence, he would,
according to %sage, fix a day for its considera-
tion.

_
Mr. Gladstone replied to the question at
more than ordinary length. In the opinion
of the Ministry, that Bill would render
it impossible for them to redeem the pledges
which they gave when they took office
in 1808, and therefore its adoption would
prevent their continuing with credit or advan-
tage, or with satisfaction to the House, to be,
responsible for the conduct of public affairs.
At the same time, he acknowledged that it
was desirable that the juigment of the House
should be taken upon the question as soon as
possible; and while announcing that he could
not interrupt the proceedings on the Ballot
Bill and some other measures, offered to con-
sider the state of public business, with a view
to finding a day—which ho admitted could
not be an early one—for the consideration of
this Bill. The conclusion of the answer was
cheered. by members on both sides of the House,
but its result was unsatisfactory to Mr.. 1 aw-
cett, who, speaking amid many cries of
" Order, " and provoking the interposition
of the Speaker, stated that the course which
had been pursued by the Government during
the last few days was fatal to the privilege of
independent members; and, gave uutice that

!le should move the adjournment of the House,
in order that he may call attention to it. Sir
H. Selwin-Ibbetson did not press the second
reading of his• Public Health in Rural Places
Bill; but the short conversation which took
place before the measure was withdrawn,
afforded to Sir C. Adderley an opportunity
to taunt the Government with want of dili-
gence in the proseeutian of their Public Health
Bill—a suggestion which was quietly repelled
by Mr. Bruce. The second reading of the
Religious Disabilities Abolition Bill was
moved by. Sir C. O'Loghlen.
The rejection of the measure was moved by
Sir T. Chambers, who, besides objecting to
the opening of the offices referred to, dwelt
upon the inconveniences which arose from the
multiplication of monasteries, and the injury
which the State sustained by the appropriation
of property to their sapport.
The amendment was seconded by Mr. W.
Johnston, who was followed on one side or thQ
other by Sir J. Gray, Mr. Holt, and Mr.
Synan.
Dr. Ball asserted that the question of super-
stitious uses affected England more than Ire-
land, and commented upon the absence of the
English law officers, whose advice he regarded
as necessary to guide the House.
Mr. rem, in supporting the second read
ing, treated the laws against monastic orders
as obsolete • but suggested that the question
of the law of superstitious uses might be made
the subject of inquiry.
Newdegate, of course, folliwed the line
taken by Mr. Chambers, and, with his usual
energy, opposed the Bill.
On the ground of want of information, Mr.
Waters moved the adjournment of the debate,
but although he challenged a division he did
not persist in his challenge, and the discussion
went on.
When Mr. Bruce came to speak for the
Government, he argaed in favour of that por-
tion of the measure abolishing the prohibition
of a Boman Catholic filling the office of Lord
Chancellor; but expressed his regret that that
provision had been mixed up with the proposed
change in the law of superstitious uses, and
his opinion that the time had not come for
making the change proposed. To the repeal
of the clauses affecting Jesuits and monastic
orders he gave his entire dssent; but in con-
sequence of the variety of subjects embraced
in it he recommended that the Bill should be
withdrawn.
After Mr. Collins had made some observa-
tions, Sir C. O'Loghlen rose to reply, and, to
the amusement of the House, which was ex-
pressed by loud cheering and much laughter,
"talked out" his own Bill. Soon after the
House adjourned.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TFLURSDAY,
The Marquis of Clanricarde gave notice
that on an early day he should call the atten-
tion of the House to the present law relating
to the relief of the poor in Ireland.
The Archbishop of York presented a Bill to
alter and revise the boundaries of the dioceses
of York and Ripon. The Bill was read a first
time.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

Mr. Crawford moved that it be an instruc-
tion to the committee on the Thames Embank-
ment, North, Bill, that they do hear the
mayor, aldermen, and commons of the City of
London on their petition in opposition to the
Bill.
Mr. Adair, as chairman of the Court of
Referees, asked the House not to assent to the
resolution, as the Corporation was fully repre-
sented. by the Committee of Sewers.
The House divided—For the motion, 145;
Against, 151; Majority against filo motion, 9.
Lord Enfield, replying to Sir C. Wingfield,
said that no further oorrespondenco had been
received on the subject of coolie emigration
from Macao, but in a report from Hong Kong
it was stated that the traffic was better con-
dusted at Macao than at Hong Kong.

TUE GOVERNMENT AND THE' DUBLIN IJNIVER-

SITY (TESTS) BILL.
Mr. Fawcett, in pursuance of the notice
which he gave on Wednesday, rose to call the
attention of the House to the course pursued
by the Government in reference to this mea-
sure. After premising that the promoters of
the Bill were not in the slightest degree
responsible for the present position of affairs, he
ventured to say that the Government, with-
out any intimation to the promoters or any
notice to the House, adopted a course of pro-
ceeding which was absolutely
'annals
a pre-
cedent in the whole political annals of this
country. When the second reading was pro-
posed the promoters of the bill thought that
the Government could not escape from a clear
and specific declaration of their views, but
inexhaustible were their sources of veiling a
clear and distinct issue on. this question.
They supported the second reading,
but said that the second half of the
bill was objectionable, and that they would
move to strike it out, treating the motion as a
vote of confidence. Never before had a
Government- ifi that House assented to the
second 'reading of the Bill, and then turned
round and „litated that one half of the measure
was objectionable, and would be treated as a
vote of want of confidence. Before the
Government treated the bill on this ground

three-fourths of the Liberal side of the House 1
were in favour of it. On the Monday night
numbers of hon. members came to him and
said that they agreed with every- clause of his
bill, but when it became a question involving.
the existence of the Government, could he ex-
pect Ahern to prefer Dublin University to a
Liberal Government? He had a proposal to
make to the Government, viz., that they would
find him a day for the disc ion of the ques-
tion some time before them he of June; and
he avowed the determination of the promoters
to presslhis question forward to a conclusion,
and if possible to extract from the Government
a distinct and clear expression of their views.
In conclusion, he moved the adjournment of
the House.
Dr. Lyon Playfair seconded the motion,
which was supported by Mr. Bouverie.

articles.title: STRIKES.
articles.text:
STRIKES.

Mr. John Smedley, of Lea Mills, Matlock
has sent us the following communication
As the question of strikes And the rela-
tions of employers and operatives is occupying
so much attention, I send you my own ex-
perience, which is at .your service should you
consider it desirable and worth inserting in
your paper. We have never had a strike, or
any disagreement with our hands in my time,
nor in my father's, or grandfather's time. We,
have been engaged in spinning and mannfac-
turing long before the commencement of this
century. My ancestors' idea was, that those
who rode inside the coach should make those
as comfortable as possible who are compelled,
from the mere accident of birth, to ride out-
side. Acting on this principle as much as
possible,% our plans with respect to the em.
ployed are as follows :—We commence work
at the mills at 6 a.m., go on till breakfast-time
8 0. The hands have opportunity in the
mill, previous to the hell ringing out, to
wash—water, soap, and towels being pro-
vided. They assemble in the dinner-house,
and find hot coffee, . or tea, sweetened and
milked, at a half-penny per pint, or Scotch
oatmeal porridge, -either with Macfie's best
golden syrup, or with half a pint of milk, at
fourpence half-penny per week. All is optional.
We keep a man cook, and assistants, and some
boys and girls to receive any food the hands
bring with them to cook. The boys and girls
wait upon the hands, and in a quarter of an
hour breakfast is generally finished: the
remaining quarter of an hour in fine weather
the hands stroll out, or if wet, read, knit, or
sew. At 8 30, a manager takes his stand at a
desk in the same room, and gives out a hymn,
then reads in the Bible, or other works of
general interest, then a short prayer, and the
choir sing while the hands disperse to their
work at 0, refreshed and cheered, and quite
alert for their occupations. The half hour
from 8.30 to 9 is given. From 12.30 to 1.30
dinner; the cooks cook anything the hands
bring. The hands wash again, in our time,
before coming out of the mill, and find their
dinners ready, consisting of various kinds of
food, bacon, meat, dough for dumplings, or
pasties, potatoes boiled or fried, and
various other things brought by them, and
tea or coffee, as at breakfast. Work again
from 1.30 till 6, except on Saturdays,
when at 12 30 the mill is closed. Men allowed
time for tea or coffee at 4 30. Christmas Day
and Good Friday all wages paid in full. Loss
of time for sickness not less than half wages
paid according to family, and when in a club
the allowance geberally brings it up to full
wages. Women and girls if in, a club, the
i
allowance makes t nearly.equal to full wages
—otherwise one-third to one-half wages
awarding to circumstances. We have hydro.
pa thio hospitals, where any hands requiring
treatment have board and lodging free, and
half wages. If ill at home they are fetched,
if they wish, to the hospitals. If any calamity
such as death in the family occurs, or if they
are detained at home from sickness in the
family, we assist them; they know always
where to apply for help and sympathy. Many
yearn ago 1 had to follow the changes con-
stantly, going on in manufacturing and go
into a class of goods more in general
demand, in which, of - course, we find
keen competition, but that did not induce
me to try to alter the policy towards the
workpeople, and I have still found it the most
profitable to keep to our plans in trying to
make them as efficient as possible for the
vvoik they have to do. I believe the present
disagreements between employers and em-
ployed is tho long neglect of consideration
for the workers, and the want of sympathy
and personal knowledge and intercourse with
*them, and now, like a neglected family, it is
bringing its natural and inevitable results, and
till this is altered masters may meet and pass
resolutions just as effective as if they passed
one that there should be fine weather for the
next three months. Not having any family
or relatives to succeelme, I have kept the busi-
ness down, and have only about 1,000 Or 1,100
hands connected with it. I could find employ-
ment for 4,000. About half.the hands are on the
premises, the others work lathe neighbourhood,
at their homes, or in shops, and. bring their
work in, on Saturdays and Mondays; when
they can have hot tea atid coffee, and bread

and cheese free. This saves them from milling
at public-houses for refreshments, at the con-
sequent risk of spending their week's earnings
and incapacitating them for their work for a
week or more which would disappoint our
customers, and we should lose the profit on
the work. By this policy we have held our
well-known position in our trade in spinning
and manufacturing merino hosiery. We
never have to ask for orders, nor money, never
make bad debts, nor draw, nor accept bills;
and as to profit, we get what should satisfy
aay reasonable expectations. We pay full
wages, the hands are smart and effective, no
man ever loses a day from drunkenness, and
rarely can a hand be tempted to leave us. We
keep a supply of dry stockings for those women
to put on who come from a distance and get
their feet wet, and every overlooker has a stook
of macintosh petticoats to lend the women
going a distance on a wet night. When Igo
amongst them, all recognise me, and it is
always a pleasure to go through the mill. I
wish I could make their lot easier, for with all
we can do, factory life is a hard one. If the
hands in any branch of the business have any
representations to make about wages or any-
thing respecting our rules and regulations
they come freely to us knowing that we are
always ready to listen to and grant any
reasonable 'request. It is a sad state of things
when masters have to combine against the
hands and the bands against the employers ;
it has just the same effect as parents combin-
ing against their children and the children
against their parents. If the children are not
what they ought to be it is very certain to be
the parents' fault in not gaining their afro-
tions and confidence. Veritas est Inagna et
prevalebit.' Truth is great and will prevail,
and nothing bat justice and truth can stand
long."

articles.title: INTERNATIONAL ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
THE INTERNATIONAL ASSOCIATION.

A fully attended' ;fleeting of the Oeneral
Council of the International Working Men's
Association was held at the Council-room,
Oxford-street, London, on Saturday; "Citizen"
Longuet in the chair. The statements made
by Mr. Baillie Cochrane in the debate upon the
International in the House of Commons were
brought under consideration, and much indig-
nation, we are informed, was expressed by
several members of the Council at what they
alleged to be the gross misrepresentation of
facts by Mr. Cochrane and other speakers. -A
manifesto was drawn up and. adopted, 'and.
ordered to be issued to the members and the
public, pointing out the "false statements"
and misrepresentations made during the debate.
This " manifesto " says :—" The gist of Mr.
Cochrane's speech was contained in the part in
' which he stated that he should be able to show
that the Commune of Paris, now the Inter-
national, was in reality one, and. that the
International Society, located in London, had
given orders to the Commune to burn Paris
and murder the hosteges. Now, what proof
of the truth of this statement did Mr. Cochrane
bring forward? Why, he added, only last
week Eugene Dupont was arrested in Paris,
where he had gone secretly from this country.
Now this Eugene Dupont was a member of the
Commune and also a member of the Inter-
national Society. Unfortunately for Mr.
Cochrane's argument, M. A. Dupont, the
member of the Commune who has been arrested
in Paris, was not a member of the Inter-
national, and M. Eugene Dupont, who is a
member of the International., was not a
member of the Commune at any time." The
manifesto then goes on to refute other state-
ments' in the speech of Mr. Cochrane. It was
signed by all the members of the Council,
50 in number, of whom 36 are Englishmenxe-
presenting various organisations of working
men and trade lkocieties.

Mr. Leatham, M.P. for Huddersfield, has
nAldressed a letter to his eonstituents, in which
h e contradicts the rumours of his retirement,
and. declares that he is warmly attached to his
constituency, which attachment he believes is
reciprocated.

A Bill for the punishment of drunkenness
has been discussed in the French Assembly.
It was opposed by M. Testelin, a medical man,
who declared it to be an attempt at legislation
which would certainly fail. Fines and im-
prisonment were of no use; it was only by
improving the moral and material condition of
the people that drunkenness was to be dimi-
nished. The Bill, too, was evidently directed
against the poor, and not against the rich, who
were more culpable when they indulged to
excess, as they knew better, and bad not the
excuse of misery. M. Laboulaye defended the
Bill, and maintained that the necessity of
penal legislation on the subject had been felt
in all times, and it might just as well be urged
that laws against murder and robbery were of
no use because they failed to altogether repress
those crimes. The first article, which contains
the principle of the Bill, was then passed; but
ultimately but little of the original measure
will probably remain, owing the amend-
ments hereafter to be brought forward. The
Bill owes its origin to the idea that.the Com-
mune was due to drink.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

The great State Funeral of the late Lord
Mayo took place yesterday at Dublin, and the
pageant was of a most magnificent and
imposing character. All business was sus-
pended, the streets were densely thronged, and
the whole city wore an air of mourning.
The provincial papers report violent thunder-
storms in the northern and midland counties
yesterday.

Yesterday being the 29th anniversary of the
birth of H.R.H. the Princess Alice, the event
was celebrated in the usual manner at Windsor.
The bells of St. George's Chapel were rung
at intervals, and a Royal salute was fired at
twelve o'clock in the Long-park.

On Wednesday a great eruption of Mount
Vesuvius commenced., and the crater had the
appearance of a vast fire. The lava descended
in several directions.

The Scotsman says that Mr. Bright is still
nervous about his health, but it is hoped that
this feeling will soon wear away. The right
hon. gentleman proceeds to the north imme-
diately, if, indeed, he .has not already left
London.

The shooting regulations and prize list of
the forthcoming great national rifle meeting
on Wimbledon-common have just been issued
by the National Rifle Association. . The meet-
ing itself will commence on Monday, July. 8,
but in order to make the necessary arrange-
ments for the thousands of riflemen who will
compete from all parts of the kingdom for the
Queen's Prize and the St. George's Challenge
Vase contests the latest date of entry has been
fixed at the contests,
of May.

Mr. Gorton, solicitor, has received a com-
munication from the Southampton admirers of
the Claimant, authorising him to provide a
carriage an& four for the conveyance of the
Claimant to his residence on being released
from custody.

The Spanish Radicals, presided over by Ruiz
Zorrilla, have met and decided to condemn
the Carlist rising, and to assist the Govern-
ment in maintaining, order. This is thought
a preliminary step Cowards reconciliation with
Sagasta.

H.R.U. Prince Arthur, accompanied by
Lieutenant Fitzgerald, returned from London
to Dover yesterday morning.
A journal of Marseilles states, that when the
new executioner arrived at Aix to carry out
the sentence on the murderer Tourres, not one
of the hotels would accommodate him, and he
was forced to ask for shelter from his former
colleague of the town, who treated him very
hospitably.

During a thunderstorm on Wednesday after-
noon, the lightning struck one of the -pinnacles
of the tower of St. George's Church, Kidder-
minster, and injured it so much that it will
Probably have to be taken down. The pinnacle
was completely twisted round, and several
pieces of stone' were thrown a considerable.
distance right over the tower.
The Irish Amnesty Association has trans-
mitted an address to Mr. Gladstone, urging
the advisability of releasing the prisoners
still enduring punishment on account of
political offences oonneeted with Ireland.

GENTLEAIEN,—I have carefully examined the
valuations of the liabilities of your Company made
by Mr. Hughes for the General, and Mr. Dewey
for the Industrial Branch. The conditions under
which the business of the two branches is con-
ducted differ materially. In the Industrial Branch
the Policies have almost all been granted for the
whole term of life; but it is found that a large pro-
portion of the whole number is kept in force for
short periods only. The Premiums on all those
Policies are payable weekly, and being collected
by the Company from the Policy-holders, such a
business necessarily involves Considerable expense,
and, therefore, the rates of Premium Must be
higher than in the General Branch. From these
circumstances it seems to me that the liabilities of
the two Branches should not be regarded in the
same manner. This, however, seems to be at
variance with the provisions of the Life Assuratice
Companies' Act, which requires that a valuation of
the whole of the liabilities shall be periodically
made, and that Schedules containing particulars
of all the outstanding risks shall be delivered to the
Board of Trade. The enormous labour attending
such an investigation in the case of your Company
has, therefore, been undertaken, and the results
are TIONV submitted.

On the 31st December, 1871, there were in force
in the General Branch 11,179 Policies for Assur-
ances of £1,700,202, including • £46,51:1 bonus
additions; 148 Immediate Annuities of £4,303 ;
38 Deferred and Contingent Annuities of £1,032,
the Premiums payable tinder these contracts
amounting to £60,669 per annum; Re-assurances
were subsisting to the amount of £35,238. There
is also a small liability arising from 25 outstanding
Policies involving the contingency of Sickness.
At the same date there were in force in the
Industrial Branch 812,208 Policies tn. As.ur-
ances of £6,531,934, the Premiums on which
amount to £288,221 annually. The average
amount assured by each Policy is £8 Os. 10d., the
average weekly Premium rather more than lid.,
the average rate of Premium being £4 Bs. 3d, per
cent. per annum. The significance of the last
fact will be understood, when it is added that less
than 4 per cent. of the Policies in force are on
lives above 60 years of age, and attention is
directed to it as tending to explain the serious
mistakes into which some persons have fallen, who
attempted to apply to this branch of your business
tests of solvency derived from the experience of
Companies whose Policies have been granted on
very different terms.
The values of the Carlisle Table of Mortality at
3 per cent. interest of the sums assured, annuities
and future premiums payable under all those con-

THE LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual weekly meeting of the board was
held on Wednesday at Guildhall, Mr. Charles
Reed, M.P., the Vice .Chairman, presiding.
Lord Mahon, M.P., introduced. by Mr. W.
H. Smith, ALP.' took his seat as one of the
members for the Westminster Division in the
place of Viscount Sandon, M.P., resigned.
Monday, the 27th of May, was fixed for the
election of a member for the Greenwich Divi-
sion, in the place of Canon Miller, resigned.
The Vice-Chairman brought up the rep/.
of the Works and General Purposes Com-
mittee, and its recommendations were agreed
to—viz., the transfer to the Board of the
Pritchard-road, Hackney, Infant Schools; the
hiring for a year of the schoel-room behind
the Methodist New Connection Chapel, Lorri-
more-street, Walworth ; rules to be observed in
planning and fitting up Board Schools; a copy
of such rules to be forwarded to the Educa-
tional Department; and future conditions and
particulars for the erection of schools to be
drawn up on the basis thereof.
• Mr. APGregor presented the report of the
Committee on Industrial Schools, showing the
number of oases dealt with before March 12.
It states that the number of certified Industrial
Schools which have agreed to receive children
sent by the Board is 30. Of these 19 are in or
near London, and 11 in the country. The
total number of children so sent is 231—viz.,
Protestant, boys, 135; girls, 19; Roman
Catholics, boys, 59; girls, 18. The health of
the children is reported as good for 131 boys
snd 27 girls; middling, for 19 boys and 7
girls; bad, for 6 boys and 1 girl. There has
been one death, a 'boy, from typhoid fever.
The conduct is reported as—Good, for 157 boys
and 20 girls; .middling, for 32 boys and 10
girls; bad, 2 boys and 4 girls. One child
absconded, but 'was captured in a day or two,
and four others who absconded were recaptured
and sent to reformatories. Mr. M‘Gregor also
brought up the report of the School Manage-
ment Committee, recommending an addition
of £5 and £lO to the salaries of probationary
and ex-pupil teachers, appointing seven
teachers at salaries ranging from £4O to £7O,
and authorising a deputation to the Educational
Department, to urge the desirableness of placing
facilities in the way of private school teachers
for obtaining certificates.
Several reports from Divisional Committee's
were considered, and visitors appointed—for
Chelsea, 4; Greenwich, 8; 'Maryleboue, 5 ;
and Southwark, 5. In the case of Greenwich
an amendment was moved to reduce the num-
ber to 6, but, after some discussion, it was
negatived by a majority of 14 to 10. Some
school manager' were also appointed, inolud-
ing those of Bemers-street, Whitechapel, and
Phcenix Temperance Hall new schools; and
Trinity Schools, East India-road.
The Rev. J. Llewelyn Davies gave notice
of his intention to niove that school fees be
not remitted or paid by the Board in any
case during the next three months.
The other business on the paper Was then
disposed of, and the Board adjourned.
